Motion: 150-250ms ease-out; live data dots pulse at 2s only when values change, with a reduced-motion static state; chart series draw in on first load (400ms) and never re-animate on filter changes.

Accessibility summary: navy 14.45:1, slate 5.59:1 on cloud; gold-navy pairs 7.66:1 both directions; gold banned as text on light; chart semantics duplicated in labels; tabular numerals and slashed zeros for instrument-grade reading.
reference_answer:
Daylight Grid identity: instrument-grade optimism for public-energy buyers.
Palette - Cloud #F5F8FC (bg), Navy #0B2545 (text 14.45:1), Slate #55657A (secondary 5.59:1), Gold #F2A900 (accent; on navy 7.66:1 and navy-on-gold buttons 7.66:1; never gold text on light surfaces), data set fixed: Navy/Gold/Mid-Blue #4A7BB5/Slate.
Type - single technical grotesk (Plex class), scale 1.25 from 16: 16/20/25/31/39, proposal covers 49/61; tabular figures, slashed zero, units at 0.9em secondary weight.
Viz - navy/gold 2px strokes, 8 percent gridlines, no gradients or dual axes, one fixed four-color data set, pattern fills for print, legends and labels always present.
Layout - 12-col dashboard grid (24px gutters, 1240px) and 760px prose measure sharing one grid; card borders #D9E2EC, one reserved popover shadow; navy proposal covers with cloud type and a gold rule.
Logo - grid-line with a daylight semicircle cut through it, 3px strokes, DAYLIGHT GRID tracked wordmark.
Motion - 150-250ms ease-out, pulse only on value change, 400ms first-draw charts, reduced-motion static states.
Accessibility - measured pairs above; chart meaning never color-only.

problem: Design the brand identity and UI foundation for a personal-savings fintech called Ledgerline. Target users are 25-40 year-olds who want calm, trustworthy progress tracking without gamified confetti. The product ships light and dark themes. Deliver positioning, a dual-theme palette with exact hex values and measured contrast ratios, typography and scale, layout foundations, key UI decisions for the money-in and progress screens, logo concept, and motion rules.
thinking: Positioning first. The category default is either playful neon (gamified saving) or austere bank blue. Ledgerline should feel like a well-kept paper ledger rendered digitally: precise, quiet, trustworthy, human. Trust for money products comes from consistency and legibility more than decoration, so the design budget goes into typography, number formatting, and contrast discipline, not illustration.

Two directions considered. Direction A, Bank Vault: navy, gold, serif, shields. Rejected: it reads institutional and intimidating, and gold-on-navy ratios are hard to keep AA for small labels. Direction B, Quiet Ledger: white and off-white surfaces, one deep ink, one teal accent that also works on dark surfaces, generous whitespace, tabular numerals everywhere. Chosen, because it is calm in light mode and can invert cleanly.

Light palette with measured ratios. Ink #101828 on white: 17.75:1 (AAA everywhere). Secondary text #667085 on white: 4.97:1 (AA body; used for labels and captions only at 14px+). Primary teal #0F766E: as button background with #FFFFFF label, 5.47:1 (AA); the same ratio applies when teal is used as text on white. Success and warning colors are handled separately and must be re-checked against white surfaces before use; they never carry meaning alone, they always ship with icons and text. Dark palette: background #0B1220, primary text #E5EAF2 at 15.50:1, accent mint-teal #2DD4BF at 10.06:1 (used for links, progress fills, and focus rings). The dark background is not pure black, which reduces halation and keeps the mint accent from vibrating.

Typography and numbers. One family for everything (Inter-class grotesk), with tabular numerals enabled globally for balances, dates, and tables. Scale ratio 1.25 from 16: 16, 20, 25, 31, 39; balances use 31-39 at weight 600 with currency symbol at 0.9em and 2px optical lift. Body line height 1.5; table rows 44px. Decimal alignment is mandatory: amounts always show two decimals, thousands separators, and right alignment in tables.

Layout. 12-column grid, 24px gutters, 1120px max content, single column under 720px. Spacing scale 4/8/12/16/24/32/48/64. Surfaces: cards on light mode are white with a 1px #EAECF0 border and no shadow; on dark mode panels are #131B2E with a 1px #1E2A44 border. Elevation is expressed by border contrast in both themes so the two themes read as siblings.

Key UI decisions. Money-in screen: amount entry is the hero (31px tabular), keypad target 56px, currency prefix fixed; a single primary button (teal, full width, 48px) follows the amount card. Progress screen: savings goal shown as a thin linear meter (6px track #EAECF0 light / #1E2A44 dark, fill teal or mint) with the exact amount and percentage as text beside it; no rings, no confetti, no streaks. Percentages round down so 99.6 percent never displays as complete. Transaction rows: date as caption (secondary 14px), merchant in ink, amount right-aligned tabular; pending states use 60 percent opacity plus a label, not color alone.

Logo concept: the letter L drawn as a ledger rule that folds into a small upward step, 2px stroke geometry on a 24px grid; the step is the only upward-motion motif in the whole identity. Wordmark in the grotesk, weight 600, letter-spacing 0.01em. App icon: the L-step in white on teal.

Motion: 150-200ms ease-out, values count up only once on first view (240ms), never on every scroll. Focus rings: 2px teal with 2px offset in light, 2px mint in dark. Respect prefers-reduced-motion by removing count-ups entirely and showing final values.

Accessibility summary: light body 17.75:1, secondary 4.97:1, white on teal 5.47:1; dark body 15.50:1, mint accent 10.06:1; all semantics duplicated in text or icons; tabular numerals for scannability; 44px minimum targets, 48px primary buttons.
reference_answer:
Ledgerline identity: calm, precise, trustworthy ledger aesthetic, no gamification.
Light theme - Ink #101828 (17.75:1 on white), Secondary #667085 (4.97:1), Teal #0F766E (buttons/labels; white-on-teal 5.47:1), Borders #EAECF0, White surfaces.
Dark theme - Background #0B1220, Text #E5EAF2 (15.50:1), Accent #2DD4BF (10.06:1), Panels #131B2E with #1E2A44 borders.
Type - single grotesk, scale 1.25 from 16: 16/20/25/31/39, tabular numerals everywhere, balances at 31-39/600, decimal-aligned tables, 44-48px targets.
Layout - 12-col, 24px gutters, 1120px max, spacing 4/8/12/16/24/32/48/64, border-based elevation in both themes.
UI - amount-first entry (56px keypad), thin linear goal meter with exact text, pending states = opacity plus label, percentages floor so 99.6 percent never shows full.
Logo - L-as-ledger-rule with a single upward step, 2px stroke, teal app icon.
Motion - 150-200ms ease-out, one-time count-ups, reduced-motion disables them.
Accessibility - verified ratios above; meaning never by color alone.

problem: X and Y are independent with Var(X) = 4, Var(Y) = 9. Find Var(X − Y). A draft answers 4 − 9 = −5, or '5 taking the absolute value.' Evaluate.
thinking: Subtracting an independent variable changes its sign but not the variance it contributes.
1. The identity is Var(X − Y) = Var(X) + Var(Y) − 2Cov(X,Y). The supplied finite variances and independence make covariance zero.
2. Therefore Var(X − Y) = 4 + 9 = 13. Equivalently, X − Y = X + (−Y), and Var(−Y) = (−1)²Var(Y) = 9.
3. Check a concrete independent example: let X be ±2 and Y be ±3 with equal probabilities. Their difference takes −1,5,−5,1 equally often, with mean zero and mean square (1 + 25 + 25 + 1)/4 = 13.
4. The draft's −5 violates the nonnegativity of variance. Taking its absolute value produces five but does not repair the formula or reproduce the verified mean square.
5. General pattern: Square coefficients in variance formulas and account for covariance explicitly; signs of coefficients affect covariance terms, not the component variances' positivity.
reference_answer:
Var(X − Y) = Var(X) + Var(Y) − 2Cov = 4 + 9 = **13** (independence kills the covariance; the sign of Y flips but variance ignores sign). The draft subtracted — yielding a negative number, impossible for a variance — and its absolute-value patch matches no formula.

**Answer:** 13.

problem: A fair coin is flipped 10 times. Find the probability that the number of heads is even.
thinking: Flipping one designated coin changes the parity of the head count, which should pair up the sequences so that each parity class holds exactly half.

1. Test the pairing idea on 2 flips: pairs under flipping the first coin are (HH, TH), (HT, TT); in each pair one sequence has an even number of heads and one odd — even count is 2 of 4, probability 1/2.
2. Verify on 1 flip: sequences H and T pair to even (T, 0 heads) and odd (H, 1 head); probability 1/2 for even as well.
3. General argument: define a pairing that takes a sequence and flips its first coin; this is an involution and the two sequences of a pair differ in the parity of the number of heads by exactly 1.
4. So exactly one sequence of each pair has an even head count, and the probability is 1/2 for every n ≥ 1, in particular for n = 10.
5. Second method, binomial sums: the number of even subsets is Σ over even k of C(10, k).
6. Add and subtract (1 + 1)^{10} and (1 − 1)^{10}: their sum equals 2Σ_{k even} C(10, k) because the odd terms cancel.
7. Values: (1 + 1)^{10} = 1024 and (1 − 1)^{10} = 0, so Σ over even k equals 512.
8. Then the probability is 512/1024 = 1/2, matching the pairing argument.
9. Check the total over both parities: even count 512 plus odd count 512 equals 1024 = 2^{10}, so nothing is lost.

10. Sanity check the smallest even case: the probability of 0 heads alone is 1/1024, and of 10 heads 1/1024 — these two extremes are included, and the many interior even counts bring the total to 512/1024.
11. Check n = 3 by hand against the formula: even subsets are sizes 0 and 2, giving 1 + 3 = 4 of 8 sequences, probability 4/8 = 1/2 — consistent with the general answer.

12. General pattern: parity questions about binomial sums are settled either by a parity-switching involution or by evaluating (1 + 1)ⁿ and (1 − 1)ⁿ; the identical computation gives the number of subsets of size divisible by 3 via cube roots of unity.
reference_answer:
Pair every sequence of 10 flips with the sequence obtained by flipping the first coin. The two members of a pair differ in the parity of the number of heads, so exactly one has an even count — hence the probability is 1/2.

Binomial check: Σ_{k even} C(10,k) = ((1+1)^{10} + (1−1)^{10})/2 = (1024 + 0)/2 = 512, and 512/1024 = 1/2.

Small-case check: for n = 3 the even counts are sizes 0 and 2, giving 1 + 3 = 4 of the 8 sequences, again 4/8 = 1/2; the parity split is always even.

**Answer:** 1/2

problem: A policy pilot: treated region's outcome rose 60 → 75; control region rose 55 → 62 over the same period. A draft: 'the policy effect is +15 points.' Evaluate and state the identification assumption.
thinking: Difference-in-differences: (75 − 60) − (62 − 55) = 15 − 7 = 8 points — the control's movement estimates what would have happened to the treated region absent the policy.
First invalid step: 'effect = +15' uses the treated region's pre/post change alone — that change mixes the policy with any common shock (economy, season, national trend) the control region isolates.
Identification assumption: parallel trends — absent the policy, treated and control would have moved in parallel; 7 points is the estimate of that shared movement.
Assumption check: inspect pre-period slopes in both regions; if they diverge before the policy, the DiD estimate inherits the divergence.
Boundary conditions: spillovers between regions (control contaminated by the policy) and composition changes over the window both break the clean 8 — name them before trusting it.
reference_answer:
DiD estimate = (75−60) − (62−55) = 8; the draft's 15 omits the counterfactual trend. Identification rests on parallel trends (check pre-period slopes); spillovers and composition shifts are the standard threats.

**Answer:** effect ≈ 8 points under parallel trends; draft's +15 confounds the common shock.

problem: A reaction runs about 2× faster per 10 °C rise. How much faster at 50 °C than at 20 °C? A draft answers '50/20 = 2.5×.' Evaluate.
thinking: We need the compounding structure: each 10 °C step multiplies the rate by ~2.
From 20 → 50 °C: three steps (30, 40, 50) → 2³ = 8×.

First invalid step: dividing temperatures (a ratio of CELSIUS values, which aren't even proportional to a physical zero) — the rule is per-STEP multiplicative, not proportional to the temperature reading.
Sanity check the draft's number's origin: 2.5× would correspond to only ~13 °C of warming under the rule — but 30 °C of warming was asked; three doublings is the consistent count.
Verify by step trace: 20 → 30: ×2; → 40: ×2 (×4 cumulative); → 50: ×2 (×8) ✓.
Self-check the rule's limits (honesty): doubling-per-10 °C is a rough Arrhenius approximation over modest ranges near room temperature — at extremes it drifts; state it as an estimate either way.
Conclusion: ≈8× faster.
reference_answer:
Three doublings: 2³ ≈ **8×** (trace: ×2, ×4, ×8 across the three 10° steps). The draft divided Celsius readings — the rule is multiplicative per step, not proportional to the temperature. (Doubling-per-10 °C is itself an Arrhenius-range approximation — label it as such.)

**Answer:** ≈8×.

problem: An assistant answers a factual question fluently and with no hedging. A draft says: 'no hesitation means it's reliable — the confidence indicates correctness.' Evaluate.
thinking: Fluency and confidence come from how the text is generated, not from verified knowledge — nothing in the process gates an answer on its truth.
So a confident, unhedged answer can be fabricated, and the inference from style to reliability is exactly the one that fails on confidently wrong outputs.
What supports trust: measured calibration, citations that can be checked, and independent verification of consequential facts.

The working split: use fluent output for drafting and writing, verification for decisions. So: unreliable inference — fluency ≠ accuracy; verify consequential claims. The pattern: confidence is not a correctness signal without calibration data.
reference_answer:
Confidence is **not a correctness signal** without calibration data: fluent, unhedged answers can be fabricated. Treat tone as presentation, verify consequential facts independently, and prefer systems whose stated confidence has been measured against accuracy. The draft inferred reliability from style — the exact inference that fails on confidently wrong outputs.

**Answer:** unreliable inference — fluency ≠ accuracy; verify consequential claims.
verification: ask for out-of-sample calibration on similar questions

problem: A uniform 20 kg beam, 4 m long, rests on supports at x = 0.5 m and x = 3.5 m. Where can a 40 kg load sit without the beam tipping? A draft: 'anywhere on the beam — the two supports carry whatever is placed, weight only adds.' Evaluate.
thinking: Beam weight: 200 N at the center x = 2; load 400 N at position p.

Two conditions: no tipping over the right support (x = 3.5), and the left support must not lift off (R_L ≥ 0). Moments about the right support: the beam weight (200 N at x = 2) has arm 1.5 m; the load (400 N at p) has arm (3.5 − p).
Taking moments about x = 3.5 (CCW positive): R_L at arm 3.0: 3R_L + 400(3.5 − p) = 300 → R_L = [300 − 400(3.5 − p)]/3.
First invalid step: 'anywhere' — R_L ≥ 0 requires 400(3.5 − p) ≤ 300 → p ≥ 2.75; left of 2.75 the left support unloads and the beam pivots on the right support.
Beyond 3.5 (past the trim): tipping immediately; so the feasible band is p ∈ [2.75, 3.5] — a 0.75 m window near the right support.
Check endpoints: p = 2.75 → R_L = 0 (boundary); p = 3.5 → R_L = [300]/3 = 100 N ✓ safely loaded.
reference_answer:
Reaction constraint: R_L = [300 − 400(3.5 − p)]/3 ≥ 0 → p ≥ 2.75; tipping past x = 3.5. Load must sit in [2.75, 3.5] m. The draft ignored reaction sign changes — supports only push.

**Answer:** p ∈ [2.75, 3.5] m; 'anywhere' fails because a support cannot pull down.

problem: A draft claims 'n² + n + 41 is prime for all n ≥ 0' after checking n = 0 through 10. Find the flaw and a counterexample.
thinking: A polynomial that produces primes for many consecutive inputs can still fail — a long run of success is not a proof, and the classic example is this very polynomial.
The failure point: n = 40 gives 40² + 40 + 41 = 1681 = 41², composite — the polynomial is engineered to self-destruct at the square of its constant.
The next failure confirms the mechanism: n = 41 gives 41² + 41 + 41 = 41 × 43 = 1763, and the factorization checks — 41 × 43 = 1640 + 123 = 1763 ✓.
So: false; n = 40 gives 1681 = 41² (and n = 41 gives 41 × 43). The pattern: a universal claim is refuted by one counterexample, and long runs of success — here forty straight — do not prove it.
reference_answer:
The checked range proves nothing about all n. The polynomial n² + n + 41 gives primes for n = 0 to 39, but it fails at n = 40: 40² + 40 + 41 = 1681 = 41², which is composite. It also fails at n = 41: 41² + 41 + 41 = 41 × 43 = 1763. One counterexample is enough to refute a universal claim.

**Answer:** false; n = 40 gives 1681 = 41² (and n = 41 gives 41 × 43)

problem: A car takes a flat circular curve of radius 50 m; the static friction coefficient is 0.7. Find the maximum speed without sliding (g = 9.8). A draft gets ≈ 18.5 m/s but argues: 'the outward centripetal force mv²/r must be balanced by friction, so μmg = mv²/r.' Evaluate the value and the reasoning.
thinking: The number is right, but the reasoning that produced it contains a conceptual error worth repairing: centripetal is a role of the net force, not an extra outward push.
The valid derivation: Newton's radial law has static friction — the only radial force — acting as the net inward force, f = mv²/r, capped at the slide threshold f = μmg.

The draft's outward centripetal force invents a force that does not exist in the ground frame and mislabels the balance; friction does not balance the centripetal force, it is the centripetal force, and weight and normal force cancel vertically so no third radial force appears. So: ≈ 18.5 m/s — valid derivation via ΣF_r = μmg = mv²/r; reject the draft's force picture. The pattern: centripetal force is a role played by real forces, never an extra one.
reference_answer:
The number is right, the reasoning is not. Centripetal is a role of the net force, not an extra outward push: the static friction is the net radial force, f_s = mv²/r, capped at μmg. Solve: v = √(μgr) = √343 ≈ 18.5 m/s (≈ 67 km/h). The draft's 'outward centripetal force' invents a force and mislabels the balance.

**Answer:** ≈ 18.5 m/s — valid derivation via ΣF_r = μmg = mv²/r; reject the draft's force picture.
verification: force inventory in the ground frame; scaling checks v ∝ √r, √μ
failure_modes: centripetal treated as an extra force

problem: Show that $\gcd(n^2+1,\ n^3+2n) = 1$ for every positive integer $n$.
thinking: The second polynomial should be reduced modulo the first, and the relation n² ≡ −1 is what makes the reduction short: multiplying by n gives n³ ≡ −n.
So n³ + 2n ≡ −n + 2n = n (mod n² + 1), and the gcd chain closes: gcd(n² + 1, n³ + 2n) = gcd(n² + 1, n) = gcd(1, n) = 1, since n² + 1 − n·n = 1.
So the gcd is 1 for every positive integer n, and the spot checks agree: n = 2 gives gcd(5, 12) = 1 ✓, n = 3 gives gcd(10, 33) = 1 ✓, and n = 4 gives gcd(17, 72) = 1 ✓.

The error to guard against is deleting n³ outright, as if n³ ≡ 0: that would wrongly produce gcd 2 at odd n, a claim n = 1 refutes immediately. The pattern: reduce powers with the relation that defines the modulus, and let the constant that remains decide.
reference_answer:
Reduce modulo $D = n^2+1$: from $n^2 \equiv -1$, multiply by $n$ to get $n^3 \equiv -n$. Hence

$$n^3+2n \equiv -n+2n = n \pmod D,$$

and $\gcd(D,\, n^3+2n) = \gcd(n^2+1,\, n) = \gcd(1, n) = 1$. So the gcd is 1 for every positive integer $n$. Check: $n = 2$: $\gcd(5,12) = 1$ ✓; $n = 3$: $\gcd(10,33) = 1$ ✓. (Dropping $n^3$ entirely — as if $n^3 \equiv 0$ — would wrongly give gcd 2 at odd $n$; $n = 1$ refutes it.)

**Answer:** the gcd is 1 for every positive integer $n$

problem: At a mountain camp 3000 m up, a draft insists 'water boils at 100 °C, that is fixed; only cooking oil changes.' Evaluate and say how cooking times are affected.
thinking: Water boils when its vapour pressure equals the surrounding pressure, so the boiling point is a pressure-dependent quantity — 100 °C is its value at one standard atmosphere, not a universal constant.
At a 3000 m camp the ambient pressure is about 70% of sea level, and water boils near 90 °C there.
The consequence: cooler boiling water cooks more slowly, so food takes longer at altitude — and the pressure cooker confirms the rule from the other side, with higher pressure and a boil near 120 °C.

So: boils below 100 °C at altitude; cooking is slower. The draft treated a sea-level value as fixed and blamed only the oil. The pattern: boiling points are set by pressure, and the kitchen is the laboratory where this shows up.
reference_answer:
The boiling point is **pressure-dependent**: water boils at 100 °C only at standard sea-level pressure; at 3000 m (~70% pressure) it boils near 90 °C, so cooking is slower there. The draft treated a sea-level value as universal. The pressure cooker (higher pressure → hotter boil) confirms the same rule from the other side.

**Answer:** boils below 100 °C at altitude; cooking is slower.
failure_modes: textbook value used outside its condition

problem: A team needs a 10× bigger dataset; a draft proposes duplicating the existing rows 10 times. Evaluate the benefit for model quality.
thinking: Duplicating rows adds no new information: the data volume grows, but the coverage of the input space does not.
The side effects are real: training reweights toward the repeated cases, and duplicates straddling the train/test split contaminate the test set and inflate the score.
What improves quality: new examples covering weak regions, real augmentation, better labels — anything that adds information rather than copies it.
Ten copies of the same row are one row. So: no real benefit — duplicates don't add information; they can corrupt evaluation. The pattern: information content matters, not row count.
reference_answer:
Duplication adds **no information**: it reweights existing examples, can contaminate train/test splits (identical rows on both sides inflate scores), and leaves the model's gaps exactly where they were. Quality gains come from new coverage — augmentation, collection, labeling. Ten copies of the same row is one row.

**Answer:** no real benefit — duplicates don't add information; they can corrupt evaluation.

problem: ΔHf(A) = −250 kJ/mol, ΔHf(B) = −180 kJ/mol; for A → B, ΔS = −100 J/(mol·K). Find ΔH and ΔG° at 298 K for A → B and assess spontaneity. A draft: 'ΔH = ΔHf(A) − ΔHf(B) = −70 kJ/mol (exothermic), so A → B proceeds spontaneously.'
thinking: Convention: ΔH(A→B) = ΔHf(products) − ΔHf(reactants) = ΔHf(B) − ΔHf(A) = (−180) − (−250) = +70 kJ/mol — the draft subtracted reactants minus products.
Sanity: B is the less-stable higher-energy compound (ΔHf less negative), so climbing to B costs +70 — consistent with endothermic.
First invalid step: two failures at once — the reversed subtraction AND the claim that ΔH's sign alone settles spontaneity.
Check the entropy term: ΔS < 0 (order increases), so −TΔS = +29.8 opposes — both terms push positive; ΔG° ≈ +99.8 > 0 → nonspontaneous at 298 K.
reference_answer:
ΔH = ΔHf(B) − ΔHf(A) = +70 kJ/mol (endothermic); ΔG° = 70 − 298(−0.1) = +99.8 kJ/mol > 0 → not spontaneous at 298 K. The draft reverses the subtraction and treats ΔH as the spontaneity test.

**Answer:** ΔH = +70 kJ/mol, ΔG° ≈ +99.8 kJ/mol; nonspontaneous at 298 K.

problem: Two different mutations in the same signaling pathway cause identical cellular phenotypes. 'They must act in the same protein complex,' concludes a draft. Evaluate and give the discriminating experiments.
thinking: Identical cellular phenotypes show functional convergence — the same output — and several topologies converge on the same output: one shared complex, a serial pathway, parallel redundant branches, or a nonspecific shared stress response.
The arrangements differ only in experiments not yet run, so the phenotype alone cannot choose: knocking out either gene and getting the same cellular result happens under every topology on the list.

The discriminating experiments: interaction assays — co-immunoprecipitation, proximity labelling, or FRET — which the shared-complex hypothesis requires and serial or parallel topologies do not; epistasis in a double mutant, where additive or worse-than-additive behaviour suggests parallel branches while saturation at single-mutant levels suggests a linear order; and rescue hierarchy experiments to order the nodes.

Until an interaction or epistasis result exists, the honest statement is: functional convergence, physical interaction undetermined. So: convergence isn't complex membership — co-IP/proximity assays plus epistasis decide, and the conclusion stays open until then. The pattern: identical phenotypes are consistent with several models, so design the experiment that separates them.
reference_answer:
Identical phenotypes show functional convergence — the same output — not a shared physical complex. The arrangements that fit equally well include one complex, one linear pathway (serial), parallel branches feeding the same process, or a nonspecific stress response; they differ only in experiments you haven't run. Distinguish them with: (1) **interaction assays** — co-immunoprecipitation, proximity labeling, or FRET — which the shared-complex hypothesis requires and parallel/serial topologies do not; (2) **epistasis** — double mutants behaving additively or worse suggest parallel branches, while saturation at single-mutant levels suggests a linear order; (3) rescue hierarchy to order the nodes. Until an interaction or epistasis result exists, the honest statement is: same phenotype, topology unresolved.

**Answer:** convergence isn't complex membership — co-IP/proximity assays plus epistasis decide, and the conclusion stays open until then.

problem: A draft argues: 'this team has the best player at every position, so it is the best team — the parts guarantee the whole.' Evaluate.
thinking: This is the composition fallacy: properties of the parts need not transfer to the whole.
Team quality depends on coordination and fit, which no position-by-position sum captures — the all-star lineup that loses is the familiar counterexample.
The same structure appears elsewhere: molecules can have properties none of their atoms has, so best at every position is evidence for a strong team, not a guarantee of one.

A valid version of the argument would add a premise that the sport's outcome is additive — and it is not. So: composition fallacy — whole-level properties aren't sums of part-level ones. The pattern: check the interactions between the parts.
reference_answer:
The inference is the **fallacy of composition**: 'best at each part' doesn't entail 'best whole' — team quality depends on coordination and fit, which no position-by-position sum captures (all-star lineups that lose are the familiar counterexample). The parts provide evidence, not a guarantee. A valid version would add an argument that the sport's outcome is additive — which it isn't.

**Answer:** composition fallacy — whole-level properties aren't sums of part-level ones.

problem: A factory's production imposes health costs on nearby residents. A draft says 'the firm already pays for its choices, so no intervention is needed — the market internalizes everything.' Evaluate the externality reasoning.
thinking: The test is whether the firm's private cost includes the residents' health costs.
1. The damage lands on third parties with no transaction, so it is a negative externality: private cost is below social cost at the margin.
2. "Pays for its choices" covers only private inputs; the residents' costs appear on nobody's balance sheet, so output exceeds the social optimum.
3. At the unregulated quantity, social marginal cost exceeds marginal benefit, a welfare loss on each extra unit.
4. Remedies: a Pigouvian tax equal to marginal external damage, cap-and-trade, or regulation.
5. General pattern: externalities are costs that cross the firm's boundary.
reference_answer:
Private ≠ social cost: residents' health damage enters no firm's accounts, so output exceeds the social optimum — a negative externality (by definition third-party costs outside the transaction). Remedies (Pigouvian tax, cap-and-trade, regulation, or liability) target the gap. The draft's 'internalizes everything' presupposes the very compensation that is missing.

**Answer:** externality misread — the firm self-pays only private costs; policy can raise welfare by pricing the external damage.

problem: Prove 30 | n⁵ − n for every integer n. A draft: 'n⁵ − n is periodic in n with period 30, so it suffices to check n = 1, 2, 3, 4, 5: values 0, 30, 240, 1020, 3120 — all divisible by 30. Done.' Critique.
thinking: The period-30 claim is real (f(n+30) ≡ f(n) mod 30), but period 30 licenses checking the 30 residues 0…29 — five values cover only 1–5, a factor-6 gap.
First invalid step: 'checking 1…5 suffices' — the check-set size and the stated period must match; residues 6…29 (and 0) are untested.
Complete route A: verify all 30 residues (computational, valid).
Complete route B: n⁵ − n = n(n−1)(n+1)(n²+1). Among n−1, n, n+1: one even and one multiple of 3 → 2·3 | factor. For 5: if 5 ∤ n(n−1)(n+1) then n ≡ ±2 (mod 5) → n² ≡ 4 → 5 | n² + 1.
Check route B on n ≡ 2: n = 2 → n²+1 = 5 ✓; n = 3 ≡ −2: 10 ✓.
reference_answer:
Valid proofs: check all 30 residues, or use factorization — 2 and 3 divide the three consecutive factors, and 5 divides n²+1 when n ≡ ±2 (mod 5). The draft's five-value check is the invalid step: its own period argument requires 30 checks, not 5.

**Answer:** proof completes via factorization (or 30-residue check); draft's '1…5 suffices' is invalid.
verification: residue case n≡±2; factor coverage of 2,3,5

problem: Three suspects; A says 'B is lying'; B says 'C is lying'; C says 'A and B are both lying.' A draft concludes 'C is the only liar.' Evaluate and solve completely.
thinking: Formalise with "truthful" variables: A ↔ ¬B, B ↔ ¬C, C ↔ (¬A ∧ ¬B).
1. The draft ("C the only liar") makes A truthful, which needs B to lie: contradiction.
2. B truthful: A lies and C lies; C's claim "A and B both lie" is false, consistent.
3. B lying: C truthful, so A lies; but A lying contradicts A ↔ ¬B. Impossible.
4. Unique solution: A lies, B truthful, C lies.
5. Check: A's "B lies" is false, B's "C lies" is true, C's "both lie" is false.
6. General pattern: encode statements as equivalences and solve by cases.
reference_answer:
Constraints: A ↔ ¬B, B ↔ ¬C, C ↔ (¬A ∧ ¬B). Solving: B truthful forces A and C to lie, and C's statement is then false — consistent. B lying forces C truthful, whose claim then requires A lying, but A would be truthful under ¬B — contradiction. Unique: A and C lie; B is truthful; the draft's 'C only' fails the very first constraint.

**Answer:** A and C are lying, B tells the truth.
ground_truth: A and C lie; B truthful
verification: substitute the solution into all three statements

problem:
```
if key not in cache:
    cache[key] = compute(key)   # compute() calls a paid API; threads run concurrently
```
A draft: 'the GIL makes this safe — the check-and-set can't interleave.' Under load, the paid API bills climb far above the number of distinct keys. Diagnose and fix.
thinking: Race window: T1 and T2 both evaluate `key not in cache` → both miss (no key yet) → both call compute → duplicate paid calls; the GIL only guarantees single-BYTE-CODE atomicity, not check-then-act atomicity around a blocking call.

The GIL detail matters both ways: dict membership and assignment are individually atomic, but compute() is a long operation that releases the GIL — the interleaving happens BETWEEN the draft's two steps.
First invalid step: 'the GIL makes this safe' — the relevant atomicity is over the composite operation; the draft reasoned about two instructions in isolation that have a gap in between.
Fix A: a global lock around check+compute (simple; serializes all keys).
Fix B: per-key locks (lock striping) or an in-flight map: store a Future/Promise in cache under the key BEFORE computing; concurrent callers await the same future — deduplicates the paid call.
Verify: two-thread test at the same key with a counting stub → paid calls = 1 after the fix, 2+ before.
reference_answer:
Check-then-act with a slow, GIL-releasing call in between: duplicates multiply with concurrent misses — the billing symptom is expected. The GIL protects individual dict operations, not the composite pattern. Fix with a lock around check+compute, or per-key in-flight futures so concurrent callers share one computation.

**Answer:** TOCTOU race — dedupe via lock or in-flight future map; test with a two-thread counting stub.
ground_truth: duplicate computes; lock or in-flight futures

problem: Evaluate Σ_{k=0}^{10} C(10, k)·2^k. A draft: 'Σ C(10,k) = 2¹⁰ = 1024, and the factor 2^k doesn't change the count, so the sum is 1024.'
thinking: Binomial theorem: Σ C(n,k)x^k = (1 + x)^n; here x = 2 → 3¹⁰.
First invalid step: dropping the 2^k — it weights each term by a different power, transforming the sum from 2¹⁰ into 3¹⁰; 'doesn't change the count' is exactly wrong for a weighted sum.
Check small cases: n = 1: C(1,0)·1 + C(1,1)·2 = 3 = 3¹ ✓; n = 2: 1 + 4 + 4 = 9 = 3² ✓ — the pattern is (1+2)^n, not 2^n.
Size sanity: 59049 vs 1024 — the weighted sum exceeds the unweighted by the mean weight ≈ (3/2)^10 ≈ 57×.
reference_answer:
Σ C(10,k)2^k = (1+2)¹⁰ = 3¹⁰ = 59049 — each term carries its own power weight. The draft summed the unweighted coefficients (2¹⁰), which corresponds to x = 1.

**Answer:** 59049; draft's 1024 dropped the 2^k weighting.

problem: A draft argues, repeating itself three times: 'X is true because Y attests to it; Y is reliable because X is true; so X is true — the attestation is backed by X's truth, which is backed by the attestation.' Evaluate the reasoning.
thinking: The argument uses its conclusion to certify the very testimony offered in support of that conclusion.
1. Its dependency graph is X supported by Y's attestation, and Y's reliability supported by X. Following either justification returns to the claim it was meant to establish.
2. Repeating that cycle three times adds no independent premise, observation, or reliability assessment. An assertion's repetition does not increase the evidence supporting it.

3. Check logical entailment by reducing the circular support to implications R → X and X → R, where R means the attestation is reliable. X = false and R = false satisfies both implications, so neither implication pair entails X.
4. This shows the argument does not establish X; it does not show X is false. Independent evidence for X or a reliability assessment of Y that does not presuppose X could repair the justification.
5. General pattern: Trace justification dependencies to their premises and distinguish a mutually supporting cycle from an argument grounded in independent evidence.
reference_answer:
X ← Y ← X is a closed support cycle: neither claim is grounded, so the pair is consistent but carries no evidential weight — and the three restatements repeat one loop. Repair requires an external anchor (independent evidence for X or for Y's reliability). Model check: every truth assignment can satisfy the loop, so it constrains nothing.

**Answer:** circular reasoning — no external support; repetition adds none.
verification: dependency-arrow diagram; model check of the loop

problem: Prove: at any party of n ≥ 2 people (friendship mutual), at least two people shook the same number of hands. A proposed proof says: 'Counts lie in {0,1,…,n−1} — that is n values for n people, so by pigeonhole two counts coincide.' Critique the proof, then give a correct argument.
thinking: The pigeonhole argument must use the right number of holes: the extremes 0 and n − 1 cannot both occur at one party, and that exclusion is what the draft skipped.

The joint exclusion: if someone shook n − 1 hands, they met everyone, so nobody shook 0. Hence the counts lie in {0, …, n − 2} or in {1, …, n − 1} depending on which case occurs, never spanning both ends at once.

Either way at most n − 1 distinct values are available for n people, and the pigeonhole principle forces a repeat — the conclusion stands, but the draft's literal n-values-for-n-people step is invalid, since it grants one hole too many.

The n = 2 check exhibits the exclusion: the pairs of counts are (0, 0) or (1, 1), and (0, 1) is impossible. So: true — at most n−1 handshake counts are achievable, so two guests share one; the draft's reasoning was invalid regardless. The pattern: check which values a quantity can take before applying pigeonhole.
reference_answer:
The conclusion is correct, but the draft's decisive step is not: the counts 0 and n−1 cannot both occur (a guest who shook every hand would have shaken the hand of a guest who shook none), so only n−1 values are available. Repair: in each of the two cases the counts fit n−1 values, and pigeonhole then forces a repeat. The n = 2 check exhibits the exclusion.

**Answer:** true — at most n−1 handshake counts are achievable, so two guests share one; the draft's reasoning was invalid regardless.
ground_truth: claim true; draft's reasoning invalid (0 and n−1 exclude each other); repair gives n−1 achievable counts
verification: check the n=2 case: (0,1) impossible; re-audit the shelf count in both branches

problem: Same-period report claims: (C1) 'Conversion rate improved from 4% to 5%.' (C2) 'Conversions fell 10%.' (C3) 'Traffic doubled.' A draft says 'all compatible — rates and counts are different measures.' Evaluate the compatibility.
thinking: We need to derive counts from rates × traffic and test C2 against them: previous = 0.04 × T, current = 0.05 × 2T = 0.10 × T → ratio 2.5 → count change +150%, already contradicting C2's 'fell 10%'.
C2 says conversions FELL 10% — directly contradicted: C1 + C3 jointly imply conversions ROSE ~150%.

First invalid step: the draft's 'rates and counts are different' is true in general — and useless here, because C1 and C3 DETERMINE the count change; 'different measures' cannot coexist with opposite directions once the arithmetic is closed.

Model check for the readers: could denominators differ (e.g., C2's 'conversions' = a different product/segment, or 'fell 10%' = conversion-per-session vs per-visitor)? Possible — which is exactly why the honest response is (a) flag the conflict as stated and (b) name the definitional reconciliations worth checking (same product? same conversion definition? same period? traffic base?).
Self-check the magnitudes: +150% vs −10% is not rounding — no plausible rounding reconciles them under one definition.
Verification: recompute with explicit numbers (T=10,000): old 400 conversions; new 1,000 → +600 (2.5×) vs C2's 360 — the gap is structural.
Conclusion: C1+C3 contradict C2 as stated; flag plus definition audit.
reference_answer:
Arithmetic closes the system: C1 (4%→5%) × C3 (traffic ×2) ⇒ conversions ×2.5 (+150%); C2's '−10%' contradicts that as stated — not a rounding or measure-type gap. Correct handling: flag the conflict AND audit definitions (same product/period, conversion definition, traffic base) since conflicting reports often hide denominator mismatches. 'Different measures' alone can't reconcile opposite directions.

**Answer:** contradictory as stated — counts must have risen ~150%; check definitions before reconciling.

problem: A model change raises overall accuracy 2% but drops a critical subgroup slice by 15%. A draft: 'ship — the aggregate improved.' Evaluate the deployment decision.
thinking: An aggregate gain can coexist with a serious subgroup regression, so it does not alone establish deployment suitability.
1. Overall accuracy averages subgroup performance with population weights. A small critical subgroup can lose fifteen percentage points while gains elsewhere increase the aggregate by two points.
2. Check an example with a 10% critical subgroup: its −15-point change contributes −1.5 points overall; a +3.8889-point gain in the other 90% contributes +3.5 points, yielding the net +2-point gain.

3. The prompt's percent language should be clarified as relative changes or percentage points, and the measured differences need subgroup sample sizes and uncertainty. The coexistence is possible either way; the example uses percentage points explicitly.

4. Compare candidate and incumbent by predefined critical-slice criteria and relevant error costs, investigate the regression, and seek a correction or a justified deployment restriction. Do not assume legal protected status or a particular harm merely from the word critical.

5. The aggregate alone cannot decide the tradeoff. This is not automatically Simpson's paradox: opposite changes in one subgroup and the pooled score need no reversal across every stratum or changing composition.
6. General pattern: Audit the weighting and decision-relevant slices behind a pooled metric, quantify uncertainty, and make deployment criteria reflect consequences rather than only the aggregate.
reference_answer:
Aggregate gains can coexist with serious slice regressions (composition effects hide cells). Before shipping: reject the aggregate-only criterion, inspect the slice table, set per-slice floors, and make the trade-off explicit (is +2% pooled worth −15% on a critical population?). The draft's 'ship' misplaces the decision boundary.

**Answer:** hold — slice-level gates and an explicit trade-off decision, not the pooled number.
ground_truth: no ship; slice gates + explicit trade-off

problem: A draft cites the Coase theorem: 'with clear property rights, parties bargain to efficiency regardless of who owns the right — so regulation is never needed.' Evaluate the inference from theorem to policy.
thinking: We need the theorem's PREMISES: zero (or negligible) transaction costs, full information, clearly assigned and enforceable rights, and a small set of parties — under those, private bargaining reaches the efficient outcome regardless of the initial allocation.

The draft's policy leap drops every premise: real disputes involve many parties (smog over a city), high bargaining costs, asymmetric information, holdouts, and enforcement gaps — precisely the conditions where bargaining FAILS and the theorem says nothing.

First invalid step: treating a conditional theorem as an unconditional policy result — 'so regulation is never needed' inverts the theorem's structure: Coase identifies WHEN markets suffice, and the failures identified by its premises are the standard textbook rationale FOR policy.

Second precision the draft also blurred: the theorem's 'regardless of who owns the right' concerns EFFICIENCY, not distribution — who holds the right changes who pays whom (a major policy question the draft erased).

Self-check with an example reading: two factory-and-fisherman parties near zero bargaining cost → Coasean bargaining plausible; a million affected residents → transaction costs dominate → policy tools (taxes, standards, liability) carry the load.
Verification frame: for any proposed private bargain, audit the four premises; each failure is a named policy rationale, not an argument against policy.
Conclusion: conditional theorem; regulation's necessity is exactly the question its premises frame.
reference_answer:
Coase holds under zero transaction costs, clear enforceable rights, full information, small numbers: then bargaining is efficient (and allocation doesn't affect efficiency — though it does affect who pays). The draft dropped all premises; large-number/frictional disputes are where bargains fail — the textbook case FOR regulation. Efficiency ≠ distribution: the right's holder matters for equity.

**Answer:** invalid inference — the theorem is conditional; its premise-failures are policy rationales, not refutations of policy.
ground_truth: conditional; premises matter; regulation not excluded

problem: Library rules: (L1) loans run 14 days; one renewal of 14 days IS allowed if no holds exist; (L2) a hold on book B was placed Mar 10; (L3) patron P borrowed B Mar 1 and renewed it Mar 14; (L4) returned Mar 30; (L5) late fee $0.50/day. What is owed? A draft: 'renewal took effect, new due date Mar 29, one day late — $0.50.' Evaluate.
thinking: The hold predates the renewal, so the renewal's eligibility condition must be checked before using a later due date.
1. Adding fourteen days to the March 1 loan gives an original due date of March 15. The book is returned on March 30.
2. The hold was placed on March 10, before the March 14 renewal. With that hold still active and no exception specified, the no-holds condition is not met, so the renewal is not authorized under L1.
3. Applying the stated policy leaves the due date at March 15. The return is fifteen days after that date, producing 15 × $0.50 = $7.50.

4. Check the draft's arithmetic separately: if an authorized renewal extended the due date by fourteen days to March 29, March 30 would indeed be one day late. Its $0.50 result depends on accepting a renewal that conflicts with the supplied eligibility rule.

5. The record's statement that the patron renewed identifies a policy discrepancy, not evidence of an unstated override. If a real library honored that renewal or the hold had been canceled, actual account liability would need clarification; neither exception is given here.
6. General pattern: Check an extension's authorization before doing date arithmetic, and flag any recorded action that conflicts with the governing rule.
reference_answer:
The hold (Mar 10) predates the renewal (Mar 14) → renewal condition failed → due date stayed Mar 15 (original 14 days). Returned Mar 30 → 15 days × $0.50 = **$7.50**. The draft accepted the renewal's occurrence without testing its legality against L1's condition and the date order.

**Answer:** $7.50 owed — the renewal was invalid (hold existed first).

problem: A draft negates 'For every x, there exists y with y > x' as 'For every x, there exists y with y ≤ x.' Correct it.
thinking: Negation pushes through quantifiers one at a time: each for-all becomes there-exists, each there-exists becomes for-all, and only the innermost predicate gets flipped.
So the negation of for every x there exists y with y > x is: there exists x such that for all y, y ≤ x — some x has no larger y.
In words: there is an x such that every y is at most x, meaning a largest element exists; the draft negated the comparison but kept both quantifiers in place.

The check on the integers: the original is true, taking y = x + 1, so the negation must be false ✓ — and the draft's version is also true on the integers, which no negation can be while the original is true. So: ∃x ∀y: y ≤ x (some x tops every y). The pattern: flipping only the inner comparison leaves the quantifiers wrong.
reference_answer:
The negation is **'there exists x such that for all y, y ≤ x'** — swap ∀ with ∃, leave the flipped predicate inside. The draft negated the comparison but kept both quantifiers, producing a statement that is true exactly when the original is true (on the integers both hold), which no negation can do.

**Answer:** ∃x ∀y: y ≤ x (some x tops every y).

problem: A service logs critical audit records with ordinary write() calls; the machine loses power seconds later and recent records are missing. A draft says 'write() succeeded, so the data was on disk — the loss is impossible.' Evaluate durability.
thinking: A successful write() only copies bytes into the operating system's page cache — the data sits in memory, not on stable storage, and a power cut discards it.
Durability needs fsync: a write(), then fsync(fd) — and fsync of the directory for a newly created file — before reporting success.
The cost is the point: fsync is slow, which is why systems batch writes deliberately; the assumption of free durability is exactly what journals and sync protocols exist to fix.
So: not durable — fsync (and directory sync) required before power-loss safety. The pattern: acknowledged is not durable, and the gap between the two is the crash window.
reference_answer:
The loss is expected: write() only copies data into the OS page cache; without **fsync** (plus a directory sync for new files), a power cut drops recent writes. 'write() returned' ≠ 'durable.' Systems that log audits pay the fsync cost deliberately — the draft's assumption of free durability is the very thing journals exist to fix.

**Answer:** not durable — fsync (and directory sync) required before power-loss safety.
verification: trace where the bytes live at each stage

problem: Lab rule: 'Safety glasses must be worn in the lab unless the person is in the designated office zone.' Question: must a person wear glasses while crossing the lab to reach the office zone? A draft says no, 'because their destination is the office zone.' Evaluate.
thinking: The exception "unless the person is in the office zone" depends on where the person is, not where they are going.
1. While crossing the lab the person is in the lab, so the glasses rule applies.
2. The exemption starts only once they are inside the office zone.
3. If destination controlled the rule, anyone heading to the office would be exempt anywhere, which would swallow the rule.
4. The text is unambiguous here; the draft stretched its scope. Where the office zone begins is a question of fact.
5. General pattern: read an exception as the text states it and do not substitute a different condition.
reference_answer:
The exception conditions on current location ('in the office zone'), not destination: while crossing, the person is in the lab → glasses required; the exemption begins only on entering the zone. The draft replaced the clause's condition with an unstated one, which would gut the rule. Note: the zone's boundary is a facts question, not interpretive license.

**Answer:** required during the crossing — the draft misread the exception's scope.
ground_truth: glasses required while crossing; exemption is locational
verification: substitute both readings and compare consequences

problem: A factory can install a filter for $10k; without it a downstream farm loses $15k. A draft: 'under polluter-pays law the filter gets installed (efficient); if the property rule favored the polluter instead, the filter would not be installed — the rule determines whether the outcome is efficient.' Evaluate.
thinking: Efficiency: filter costs 10 < damage 15 → installing is the efficient outcome regardless of the legal rule.
If the farm holds the right: polluter filters (or pays ≥ 10k equivalent) → filter stands.
If the factory holds the right: the farm can pay the factory up to 15k (its avoided damage) to install — the factory accepts anything ≥ 10k → filter still stands (any split of the 5k surplus).

First invalid step: 'the rule determines efficiency' — with frictionless bargaining the RULE fixes who pays, not whether the filter exists; the 5k surplus exists either way and gets split by bargaining.

Qualifier that keeps the law relevant: with transaction costs (many farms, holdout, litigation), the allocation CAN stick — the draft's error is stating it as the general case rather than a friction case.
Conclusion: efficiency invariant under zero transaction costs; the draft conflates distribution with efficiency.
reference_answer:
Filter installed under both rules when bargaining is frictionless (cost 10 < damage 15): the rule changes who pays, not the efficient outcome. Transaction costs can freeze inefficient allocations — the caveat, not the rule. The draft confused distribution with efficiency.

**Answer:** efficiency is rule-invariant under costless bargaining; only frictions let the rule decide — draft's claim overgeneralizes.
ground_truth: filter either way without frictions; rule affects distribution
verification: surplus split analysis under both rules

problem: In triangle ABC: angle A = 30°, side a = 5 (opposite A), side b = 8. A draft finds sin B = 0.8 → B ≈ 53.1° and reports a unique triangle. Evaluate completeness (SSA case).
thinking: The sine law gives two supplementary angles here, and both leave a positive third angle.
1. From a/sin A = b/sin B, obtain sin B = 8 sin30°/5 = 0.8. The two possibilities in (0°,180°) are B₁ = arcsin(0.8) ≈ 53.1301° and B₂ = 180° − B₁ ≈ 126.8699°.
2. With A = 30°, the corresponding third angles are C₁ = 180° − 30° − B₁ ≈ 96.8699° and C₂ ≈ 23.1301°. Both are positive, so neither angle-sum constraint excludes a solution.
3. Check the remaining side from the sine law: c = 10 sin C. The two values are approximately 9.9282 and 3.9282, which both satisfy 8 − 5 < c < 8 + 5, the triangle inequalities.
4. A direct geometry check gives c = 8 cos30° ± √(5² − (8 sin30°)²) = 4√3 ± 3, reproducing those positive lengths. Thus the configurations are distinct and both valid.
5. The draft gives one legitimate triangle but leaves out the obtuse-B alternative. Sine inversion alone cannot establish uniqueness because supplementary angles share the same sine.
6. General pattern: In an SSA triangle, enumerate sine's supplementary candidates, test positive remaining angles, and verify any surviving configurations with side geometry.
reference_answer:
SSA ambiguity: sin B = 0.8 gives B ≈ 53.1° AND 126.9°; both survive the angle-sum test (C ≈ 96.9° and 23.1°) — **two valid triangles**. Uniqueness would need A ≥ 90° or a ≥ b. The draft discarded the obtuse supplement.

**Answer:** two triangles (B ≈ 53.1° or 126.9°).
verification: angle-sum feasibility for both supplements; uniqueness conditions

problem: A draft computes the power dissipated by a 6 Ω resistor across a 12 V supply as 'P = V/R = 12/6 = 2 W.' Check the calculation.
thinking: V/R is a current, not a power: dividing volts by ohms gives amperes, and the draft then labelled the result in watts.
The right formulas: I = V/R = 12/6 = 2 A, and P = VI = 12 × 2 = 24 W; the alternatives agree — P = V²/R = 144/6 = 24 W and P = I²R = 4 × 6 = 24 W.
The units tell the story: V/R is amperes, while watts are volts times amperes, and the two differ by a factor of V — the factor of 12 that the draft dropped.

The sanity check: 2 A at 12 V dissipating only 2 W would need 1 V, not 12. So: P = V²/R = 24 W (V/R gives the current, 2 A). The pattern: cross-check any power with two of the three formulas, and read the units before believing the number.
reference_answer:
The formula is wrong: V/R = 2 is the current (2 A), not the power. P = V²/R = 144/6 = **24 W**, confirmed by P = VI = 12×2 = 24 W and P = I²R = 4×6 = 24 W. The draft dropped a factor of 12 by using the current formula for power.

**Answer:** P = V²/R = 24 W (V/R gives the current, 2 A).

problem: A draft says: 'An observational study found fewer heart attacks among patients taking drug X; therefore my patient should start drug X — the evidence supports it.' Evaluate the inference chain.
thinking: The chain has three links — association, causation, treatment decision — and each needs its own evidence; the draft jumps from the first to the third in a single sentence.

The first break is at association to causation: observational users may differ systematically — healthier baseline, better access to care, better adherence to other treatments — so fewer events do not establish protection, and selection can distort the comparison beyond the confounders.

What would change the assessment: randomized-trial evidence for this drug and endpoint, or a well-controlled study with adjusted effect estimates in patients like this one; and even then the patient layer matters — baseline risk, contraindications, interactions, preferences.

So: the observational finding supports a hypothesis, not a prescription — causality and patient-specific fit are unestablished. The defensible statement is that the study shows an association worth investigating. The pattern: association to causation to treatment decision are three separate links, and each needs evidence.
reference_answer:
The chain breaks at association → causation: observational users may differ systematically (healthier baseline, better access, adherence), so fewer events don't establish protection. A treatment recommendation also needs the effect size, the population studied, and this patient's contraindications — none supplied. The defensible statement is that the study shows an association worth investigating; acting on it requires randomized or well-adjusted evidence plus an individualized risk-benefit judgment.

**Answer:** the observational finding supports a hypothesis, not a prescription — causality and patient-specific fit are unestablished.

problem: Prove that $\gcd(n^2+n,\, 2n+1) = 1$ for every positive integer $n$.
thinking: A common divisor of two numbers divides every integer combination of them, so the strategy is to build a combination equal to 1.
Let d divide both n² + n and 2n + 1; then d divides (2n + 1)², and also 4(n² + n) = 4n² + 4n = (2n + 1)² − 1.
Subtracting the two multiples: d | (2n + 1)² − 4(n² + n) = 1, so d = ±1 and the gcd is 1 for every n — no case analysis needed.

The checks: n = 2 gives 6 and 5, coprime ✓; n = 5 gives 30 and 11, coprime ✓. An equivalent route: gcd(n, 2n + 1) = gcd(n + 1, 2n + 1) = 1, and a product is coprime to c exactly when each factor is. So: gcd(n²+n, 2n+1) = 1 for all n. The pattern: to prove coprimality, combine the two numbers so the combination produces the constant 1.
reference_answer:
Let $d$ be a common divisor of $n^2+n$ and $2n+1$. Then $d \mid (2n+1)^2$ and, multiplying $n^2+n$ by 4,

$$d \mid 4(n^2+n) = 4n^2+4n = (2n+1)^2 - 1.$$

Subtracting: $d \mid (2n+1)^2 - 4(n^2+n) = 1$, so $d = \pm 1$ and the gcd is 1 for every $n$.

(Equivalently: $\gcd(n, 2n+1) = \gcd(n+1, 2n+1) = 1$, and a product is coprime to $c$ exactly when each factor is.)

**Answer:** $\gcd(n^2+n,\, 2n+1) = 1$ for all $n$

problem: Find the quotient and remainder when $n^4 + 2n^3 + 4n^2 + 4n + 3$ is divided by $n^2 + n + 1$.
thinking: Polynomial division is finished only when the remainder has smaller degree than the divisor, so subtract multiples of the divisor until that holds.
The steps: n²(n² + n + 1) = n⁴ + n³ + n² leaves n³ + 3n² + 4n + 3; then n(n² + n + 1) = n³ + n² + n leaves 2n² + 3n + 3; the remainder still has degree 2, so subtract 2(n² + n + 1), leaving n + 1.
So the quotient is n² + n + 2 and the remainder is n + 1, with degree 1 < 2 ✓.

The verification by multiplying back: (n² + n + 1)(n² + n + 2) = n⁴ + 2n³ + 4n² + 3n + 2, and adding n + 1 returns the dividend ✓. The numeric check at n = 2: dividend 59, divisor 7, quotient 8, and 8 · 7 + 3 = 59 with remainder n + 1 = 3 ✓. So: quotient n²+n+2, remainder n+1. The pattern: the remainder must have degree strictly below the divisor's.
reference_answer:
Carry the division through:

$$n^4+2n^3+4n^2+4n+3 = (n^2+n+1)(n^2+n+2) + (n+1).$$

Verification: $(n^2+n+1)(n^2+n+2) = n^4+2n^3+4n^2+3n+2$ (multiply out), and adding $n+1$ returns the dividend. The remainder $n+1$ has degree $1 < 2$ ✓, so the quotient is $n^2+n+2$ and the remainder is $n+1$. Check at $n = 2$: $59 = 8\cdot 7 + 3$ ✓.

**Answer:** quotient $n^2+n+2$, remainder $n+1$

problem: An observational study finds regular exercisers have lower depression rates. A draft writes: 'exercise prevents depression; also, depressed people are probably just lazier, so reverse causation is ruled out.' Evaluate both claims.
thinking: A cross-sectional association between exercise and lower depression is compatible with both directions — exercise reducing depression, and depression reducing exercise — and the data alone cannot say which.
The reverse direction is mechanistically expected: reduced activity is itself a symptom of depression, so reverse causation is live, not something to wave away.

The draft's dismissal — calling depressed people lazier — is not evidence, and it inverts what depression does; confounders such as social support and general health could produce the pattern as well.

What balance is possible: independent support from intervention trials showing modest symptom reductions, so the protective direction is defensible as a moderate effect — not as proof from this study. So: the claim as stated overreaches — reverse causation and confounding are live; direction rests on trial evidence, not this study. The pattern: ask what design would separate the two directions.
reference_answer:
The association alone can't decide direction: depression reduces activity (reverse causation is mechanistically expected), and confounders (social support, health) could produce the pattern. The draft's 'lazier' dismissal is not evidence — worse, it inverts what depression actually does. That said, the protective direction has independent support from intervention trials showing modest symptom reductions; the defensible statement is 'randomized evidence supports a moderate effect,' not 'this correlation proves it, and the reverse is obviously false.'

**Answer:** the claim as stated overreaches — reverse causation and confounding are live; direction rests on trial evidence, not this study.
ground_truth: association can't fix direction; trials support modest effect
verification: separate cross-sectional limits from intervention evidence

problem: Three market reports on the same sector: A says the 2022 market was $10B (software only); B says $12B (software + services); C says 2023 growth was 15% (units shipped, not revenue). A draft: 'average the figures → about $11B for 2022.' Evaluate.
thinking: Scope audit: A and B differ by construction — B adds services; their two numbers are not two measurements of one quantity but measurements of two quantities.
C's 15% is a different UNIT (units vs dollars) and a different YEAR (growth vs level) — it belongs to neither comparison.
First invalid step: averaging — the mean of incommensurable definitions produces a number that describes nothing; it is neither software-only nor software+services.

Correct synthesis: report the scope fork ($10B software; $12B incl. services for 2022), note C adds a unit-growth datapoint not revenue, and flag that no single number is supported without choosing a definition.
Check consistency where possible: does B − A ≈ a plausible services share? $2B on $12B ≈ 17% — plausible; use that as a coherence check, not as reconciliation of the total.
If the user needs one number: state the chosen definition explicitly (and why), e.g., 'software-only = $10B,' rather than fusing.
reference_answer:
The figures measure different things (scope, unit, year) — averaging manufactures a chimera. Supported output: A $10B software-only; B $12B incl. services; C 15% unit growth in 2023; pick a definition explicitly if one number is required. The $2B gap reads as a plausible services slice (~17%).

**Answer:** incommensurable — report the scope fork, no average.

problem: An object dropped from rest falls the last 20 m in exactly 1 s. Find the total height of the fall. Take g = 10 m/s$^2$.
thinking: Twenty metres in the last second is an average speed of 20 m/s over that second, and for uniformly accelerated motion the average speed over an interval equals the speed at its midpoint — that single fact fixes the total time.
So the speed is 20 m/s at the midpoint of the last second, which occurs at t = v/g = 2 s from release; the last second ends half a second later, at T = 2.5 s.
Total height: H = ½gT² = 5 × 6.25 = 31.25 m.

The mechanics check recomputes the last second directly: the speed at 1.5 s is 15 m/s and at 2.5 s it is 25 m/s, so the distance is 15 × 1 + ½ × 10 × 1 = 20 m ✓. The tempting misreading is treating 20 m/s as the final speed, which gives T = 2 s and H = 20 m — inconsistent, since a 20 m fall covers only 15 m in its final second. The pattern: use the midpoint-speed property of uniform acceleration.
reference_answer:
The average speed over the final second is 20 m/s, and for uniformly accelerated motion it is the mean of the endpoint speeds:

$$\frac{v(T-1) + v(T)}{2} = \frac{g(T-1) + gT}{2} = g\left(T - \tfrac12\right) = 20 \;\Rightarrow\; T = 2.5\ \text{s}.$$

Hence $H = \tfrac12 gT^2 = 5(2.5)^2 = 31.25$ m. Treating 20 m/s as the *final* speed gives T = 2 s and H = 20 m — inconsistent: a 20 m fall has a final-second distance of only 15 m. Check: speeds 15 → 25 m/s across that second give distance $15 + 5 = 20$ m ✓.

**Answer:** $H = 31.25$ m

problem: A pendulum bob of mass 0.3 kg is released from rest with the string horizontal (length $L = 2$ m). Find its speed at the lowest point. Take g = 10 m/s$^2$.
thinking: Released from the horizontal, the bob starts a full string length above the lowest point, so the drop is exactly L — and energy conservation does the rest.
The drop in general is L(1 − cos θ) measured from the vertical; for a horizontal release θ = 90°, so the drop is L(1 − 0) = 2 m, genuinely the full length.
Energy: ½mv² = mgL gives v = √(2gL) = √(2 × 10 × 2) = √40 ≈ 6.32 m/s.

The checks: for a release at angle θ the drop L(1 − cos θ) vanishes at θ = 0 and is largest for a horizontal release ✓, and the tension at the bottom would be T = mg + mv²/L = 3 + 0.3 × 40/2 = 9 N. The trap to name: L sin θ is the horizontal displacement, not the drop — at θ = 90° the two expressions coincide, so the wrong rule survives this special case, but at 60° it would claim a drop of 0.87L instead of 0.5L. The pattern: the vertical drop of a pendulum is L(1 − cos θ).
reference_answer:
Released from the horizontal, the bob's vertical drop to the lowest point is the full length $L$:

$$mgL = \tfrac12 mv^2 \;\Rightarrow\; v = \sqrt{2gL} = \sqrt{2 \cdot 10 \cdot 2} = \sqrt{40} \approx 6.32\ \text{m/s}.$$

For a general release angle θ from the vertical the drop is $L(1-\cos\theta)$ — not $L\sin\theta$ (that is the horizontal displacement). Here θ = 90° makes them equal, so the answer would survive the wrong rule — but the rule is invalid (at 60° it would claim drop 0.87L instead of 0.5L). Check: θ → 0 gives v → 0 ✓.

**Answer:** $v = \sqrt{40} \approx 6.32$ m/s

problem: How many ways can you choose 2 disjoint unordered pairs from 6 distinct people? A draft answers C(6,2)·C(4,2) = 90. Evaluate.
thinking: Choosing the two pairs in succession labels their order, while the requested collection of pairs is unordered.
1. Choose the first unordered pair from six people in C(6,2) = 15 ways, then the second from the four remaining people in C(4,2) = 6 ways. This gives ninety ordered pair-selections.
2. Every disjoint pair collection appears twice, once with either pair chosen first. Divide by 2! to obtain ninety divided by two = 45.

3. Check independently: choose the four participating people in C(6,4) = 15 ways. Each set of four has three pairings, found by choosing one person's partner among the other three; the final pair is forced. Thus 15×3 = 45.
4. The unordered status within each pair is already handled by combinations. Only the order between the two pairs still needs removal; the two unused people are fixed by the participants.
5. General pattern: Identify which groupings are labeled and which are symmetric, remove each overcount once, and verify with a different representation of the same objects.
reference_answer:
45: C(6,2)·C(4,2)/2 = 90/2 (pair slots are unordered); independent route: C(6,4)·3 pairings = 45 ✓. The draft left the 2! slot-overcount in. Micro-check: 4 people into two pairs = 3.

**Answer:** 45.

problem: A log pipeline reads files as BYTES, slices the first 20 bytes of each line, then decodes to text; some lines raise UnicodeDecodeError or show mojibake. A draft: 'byte slicing is safe — 20 is 20.' Evaluate.
thinking: Byte count and text-character count differ in multibyte encodings, so a fixed byte cut can split an encoded character.
1. Under UTF-8, some characters occupy multiple bytes. A twenty-byte prefix is not necessarily twenty Unicode code points or twenty displayed grapheme clusters.

2. Check the line 'a' repeated nineteen times followed by 'é': its UTF-8 encoding has twenty-one bytes, and the first twenty contain only the first byte of é. Strict decoding raises UnicodeDecodeError because the sequence is incomplete.

3. Decode the complete line with its declared encoding, then slice text if the limit is in code points. For user-visible characters, grapheme-aware segmentation may be needed because combining marks and emoji can span several code points.

4. If the requirement is a byte budget, truncate only at valid encoding boundaries and define how incomplete or invalid input is handled. Replacement or ignore policies can conceal errors or lose data and must be chosen deliberately.

5. A truncated valid UTF-8 prefix causes a decoding error under strict decoding, not necessarily mojibake. Garbled text can also come from decoding with the wrong encoding, so inspect both slicing and encoding selection.
6. General pattern: Specify the unit and encoding at every boundary, and verify truncation with a character whose multibyte representation crosses the cut.
reference_answer:
Byte slicing splits multi-byte characters → decode errors/mojibake. Fix: decode whole lines first (declared encoding), then slice by characters; for byte budgets, cut on verified boundaries. Test with a multi-byte character straddling byte 20. State the unit (bytes vs characters) at every boundary.

```python
line = raw_line.decode('utf-8', errors='replace')  # policy explicit
head = line[:20]                                     # character slice
```

**Answer:** unsafe at encoding boundaries — decode then slice (or boundary-aware byte cuts).
ground_truth: byte slice splits characters; decode first

problem: A mass–spring oscillator has period 1.00 s on Earth. It is taken to the Moon, where the gravitational field is 1/6 as strong. Find its period there.
thinking: For a mass on a spring the restoring force is the spring's, so the period T = 2π√(m/k) contains the mass and the stiffness — and no g at all; the question is a trap unless that absence is noticed.
Gravity only shifts the equilibrium position, by mg/k, so g merely decides where the mass hangs, while the oscillations about that equilibrium keep the same frequency.
So on the Moon the period is unchanged: 1.00 s (unchanged).

The distinctions check out: in free fall (g → 0) the spring–mass oscillator keeps its period, while the pendulum's period would diverge — the T ∝ 1/√g law belongs to the pendulum, where gravity is the restoring force. The pattern: ask what provides the restoring force; if it is not gravity, the period does not depend on g.
reference_answer:
For a mass–spring oscillator the restoring force is the spring's, and the period is

$$T = 2\pi\sqrt{\frac{m}{k}},$$

which does not contain $g$ — so on the Moon the period remains **1.00 s**. Gravity only shifts the equilibrium position (the spring hangs $mg/k$ lower); the oscillations about that equilibrium keep the same frequency. The $T \propto 1/\sqrt{g}$ law belongs to the pendulum, where gravity is the restoring force. Check: $g \to 0$ (free fall) leaves the spring–mass period unchanged, while the pendulum's would diverge ✓.

**Answer:** 1.00 s (unchanged)

problem: A draft writes `if arr == 5: ...` where arr is a NumPy array, and claims it works 'for arrays and scalars alike.' Evaluate and fix.
thinking: `arr == 5` on a NumPy array compares elementwise and returns a boolean array, while `if` needs a single truth value.
1. For an array with several elements, `if arr == 5` raises ValueError ("truth value of an array is ambiguous").
2. A length-1 array passes, so the bug can survive single-element tests and fail on real data.
3. Fix by stating the intent: `(arr == 5).any()` for any match, or `(arr == 5).all()` for every element.
4. Check: np.array([1,5,3]) fails without a reduction; np.array([5]) works; the two fixes differ on the first array.
5. General pattern: make the reduction explicit when array and scalar semantics differ.
reference_answer:
`arr == 5` is an elementwise boolean array; `if` on multi-element arrays raises ValueError('truth value is ambiguous'). Use explicit reductions: `(arr == 5).any()` or `.all()` per intent. Length-1 arrays mask the bug — which makes it worse, not better.

**Answer:** replace with `(arr == 5).any()` (or `.all()`); the draft's claim fails at runtime.
verification: run on multi-element and length-1 arrays

problem: 2 L of H₂ and 2 L of O₂ (same T, P) react to form water vapor. Volumes after reaction? A draft: 'both gases are consumed 1:1 (2 L + 2 L) → 4 L of water vapor.'
thinking: Equation: 2H₂ + O₂ → 2H₂O — the stoichiometric gas ratio is 2:1, not 1:1 (Avogadro: volumes follow mole ratios at the same T, P).
2 L H₂ needs 1 L O₂; O₂ is in excess: leftover 1 L O₂; water formed = 2 L (2 H₂ → 2 H₂O by ratio).
First invalid step: 'consumed 1:1' — the draft read the coefficients as one-to-one; the 2 before H₂ and 2 before H₂O looked symmetric, and O₂'s coefficient 1 was ignored.
Final volumes: 2 L H₂O + 1 L O₂ = 3 L total.
Check by atoms: 2 L H₂ = 2 units H₂ → all H → 2 H₂O ✓ needs 1 unit O₂; 2 O₂ − 1 consumed = 1 O₂ left ✓ balances.
reference_answer:
Ratio 2:1: 2 L H₂ consumes 1 L O₂ → 2 L H₂O + 1 L O₂ left = 3 L total. The draft used a 1:1 ratio from misread coefficients and would also have failed the atom check.

**Answer:** 3 L (2 L water vapor + 1 L oxygen); draft's 4 L ignores the 2:1 stoichiometry.

problem: Prove n! ≤ nⁿ for every positive integer n. A draft says 'the factorial grows slower than the power, so it holds for all n.' Evaluate and prove properly.
thinking: Each factor in n! is at most n, giving a direct pointwise comparison with n copies of n.
1. For a positive integer n, write n! = ∏ from k = 1 to n of k. Each k satisfies 0 < k ≤ n.
2. Multiplying these n nonnegative inequalities gives n! ≤ ∏ from k = 1 to n of n = nⁿ. The factor comparison proves the claim for every n, without an asymptotic argument.
3. Check equality: at n = 1, both sides equal one. For n ≥ 2, the first factor one is strictly less than n and all other factors are positive and at most n, so the product inequality is strict.
4. A small numerical check gives n = 3: 6 < 27. The draft's general growth-language does not establish every finite case, while the pointwise proof also supplies the exact equality condition.
5. General pattern: Prove product bounds by comparing corresponding positive factors, and separate pointwise inequalities from statements about eventual growth rates.
reference_answer:
Each of the n factors of n! is ≤ n, so n! ≤ nⁿ, strict for n ≥ 2 (equality only at n = 1). The draft offered an asymptote, not a proof. Spot checks: 3! = 6 ≤ 27; 5! = 120 ≤ 3125.

**Answer:** proved by the identical-factor bound; equality iff n = 1.

problem: Count the nondecreasing sequences of length 3 with entries from {1,…,5} (e.g., 1,3,3). A draft answers 5³ = 125. Evaluate.
thinking: A nondecreasing triple is uniquely determined by its multiset of entries.
1. Let ci count occurrences of value i for i = 1 through 5. Nondecreasing order gives exactly one sequence for each nonnegative integer count vector with c₁ + ⋯ + c₅ = 3.
2. Stars and bars gives C(3 + 5 − 1,5 − 1) = C(7,4) = 35 count vectors, hence thirty-five nondecreasing sequences.

3. Check by multiplicities: all entries equal gives five; exactly two distinct values gives C(5,2)×2 = 20, because either value can occur twice; three distinct values gives C(5,3) = 10. The disjoint cases total 5 + 20 + 10 = 35.
4. The draft's 5³ = 125 counts all ordered triples, including decreasing ones. Dividing by 3! would not fix it because repeated-entry multisets have different numbers of permutations.
5. General pattern: For sorted sequences with repetition, count multiplicities or multisets directly and verify with cases for repeated values.
reference_answer:
Nondecreasing ↔ multiset: C(7,3) = **35** (strictly-increasing bijection xi + (i−1) over {1..7} ✓). Analogue: length-2, 3 symbols gives 6, not 9. The draft counted all orderings.

**Answer:** 35.

problem: A cache hashes keys to 10 servers via key_hash mod 10. The team adds an 11th server 'to scale' using mod 11. A draft: 'each server keeps most of its keys — the change is gradual, like consistent hashing.' Evaluate the cache impact.
thinking: Compute the real remap rate: a key stays put iff its residue mod 10 equals its residue mod 11; over the 110-residue cycle, that holds only for the 10 residues where both agree → P(stay) = 10/110 = 1/11 ≈ 9%.
So ≈ 91% of keys move to a different server — a near-total cache invalidation, not a gradual shift.
First invalid step: 'like consistent hashing' — consistent hashing remaps ≈ 1/(N+1) ≈ 9% of keys; mod-N remaps ≈ N/(N+1) ≈ 91%; the two schemes behave oppositely.
Operational consequence: origin database hit by ~91% cold misses at once — the classic stampede from modulo hashing.
Fix: consistent hashing (or rendezvous/highest-random-weight) makes node additions cost ≈ 1/(N+1); if staying on mod-N, expect and pre-warm for a full-cycle reshuffle.
reference_answer:
mod-10 → mod-11 moves ≈ N/(N+1) ≈ 91% of keys (stay iff residues mod 10 and 11 coincide: 10/110 ≈ 9% stay). That is the opposite of consistent hashing's ≈ 9% remap — the draft's 'gradual' expectation inverts the actual behavior and invites a stampede.

**Answer:** ~91% of keys remap (not gradual); use consistent hashing for 1/(N+1) movement.

problem: Find the smallest integer n > 2026 such that n ends with the four digits 2026 (i.e., n ≡ 2026 mod 10⁴) and 2026 | n. A draft: 'Write n = 2026k and require 2026k ≡ 0 (mod 10 000), so 5000 | k; the smallest such k > 1 is 5000, giving n = 10,130,000.' Critique and repair.
thinking: Re-derive the condition: n = 2026k and 'ends in 2026' means n ≡ 2026 (mod 10⁴) — a congruence to 2026, not to 0.

First invalid step in the draft: requiring 2026k ≡ 0 (mod 10 000) — that says 'the number is a multiple of 10 000', not 'ends with the digits 2026'; its claimed answer 10,130,000 ends in 0000 and fails the stated condition outright.
Check: 2026 × 5001 = 10,130,000 + 2026 = 10,132,026 ✓ ends in 2026 ✓ divisible by 2026 ✓; no smaller k exists because k ≡ 1 (mod 5000).
reference_answer:
The condition is n ≡ 2026 (mod 10⁴) with n = 2026k: 2026k ≡ 2026 gives 5000 | (k − 1); smallest k > 1 is 5001, so n = 2026 × 5001 = 10,132,026 (the draft's ≡ 0 congruence produces 10,130,000, which ends in 0000).

**Answer:** n = 10,132,026.
verification: direct product check + uniqueness of k mod 5000

problem: A city votes on a public project's spending level; a draft: 'the majority's choice maximizes social welfare.' Evaluate with the median voter theorem.
thinking: We need what majority voting aggregates: under single-peaked preferences, the winning level is the MEDIAN voter's preferred level — a positional outcome, not a welfare maximum.
Welfare (total surplus) would weight INTENSITIES — someone who values the project enormously counts as one vote; the median outcome ignores how far the tails sit from it on each side.

First invalid step: 'majority = optimal' — the vote identifies the pivotal preference, not the sum of surpluses; misalignment is endemic (minorities with strong stakes lose to indifferent majorities, and vice versa).
