Layout. Web: 12-column grid, 24px gutters, 1160px max, with an editorial split hero (story left, product right, 45/55). Spacing 4/8/12/16/24/32/48/64. Cards are butter-toned with 1px #E3CFA6 borders and 8px radius; photography keeps a warm white balance and natural shadows, no vignettes. The flagship's in-store materials use the same grid translated to print: menu boards at 40cm x 60cm with 35mm margins, category labels in the sans caps, prices right-aligned tabular.

Packaging-to-web consistency: the same three-question label runs everywhere, What is it, When was it baked, Who baked it, set in a fixed stack with the sans for facts and the serif for the product name; the web product page uses the identical stack so shelf and screen are interchangeable. Anniversary items carry a small brick-red roundel with the year set in the serif.

Components. Primary button: brick fill with butter text (5.49:1), 48px height. Secondary: 1.5px cocoa outline. Order tickets and email receipts reuse the label stack. Menu filter chips: outlined cocoa with cocoa text, active state fills cocoa with butter text (the same 11.74:1 pair inverted).

Logo concept: a monogram HT where the crossbar of the H extends into a wheat stalk with three grains, drawn at 2.5px stroke on a 24px grid; the original painted sign's script survives as a secondary heritage lockup used only for the story page and packaging seal. The primary modern lockup is the monogram plus HARTMANN & TOCHTER in the modern sans caps.

Motion: 150-200ms ease-out fades and 4px rises, a single oven-timer-like loading indicator (a rotating roundel), no bouncing. prefers-reduced-motion disables the rise and the rotating indicator in favor of a static mark.

Voice: warm, specific, unhurried; provenance sentences with dates and people, prices stated plainly, no exclamation marks. Microcopy carries the three questions everywhere: the cart confirms bake time, the footer names the bakers.

Accessibility summary: cocoa 11.74:1, muted 5.36:1, brick 5.49:1 on butter and butter-on-brick 5.49:1 verified; sage restricted to decoration; category caps never below 12px; print menu tested at 3m viewing distance.
reference_answer:
Hartmann & Tochter rebrand: modernized craft, not sepia nostalgia.
Palette - Butter #F7E9C8 (bg), Cocoa #37281F (text 11.74:1), Muted #6E5B49 (secondary 5.36:1), Brick #A03C2B (accent and primary action; 5.49:1 on butter; butter-on-brick 5.49:1), Sage (decoration only), label border #E3CFA6.
Type - heritage serif (Playfair class) for wordmark, products, story; utilitarian sans (Work Sans class) for menus, prices, UI; scale 1.25 from 16: 16/20/25/31/39; tabular prices; caps only 12-14px with 0.08em tracking.
Layout - 12-col, 24px gutters, 1160px max, 45/55 editorial hero; spacing 4/8/12/16/24/32/48/64; menu boards share the same grid at 40x60cm.
Signature element - the three-question label (What it is / When baked / Who baked) identical on packaging, web, tickets.
Logo - HT monogram whose H crossbar grows a three-grain wheat stalk, 2.5px strokes; script heritage seal reserved for story and packaging.
Motion - 150-200ms fades, one roundel loader, reduced-motion static.
Accessibility - measured pairs above; sage decorative-only; menu legibility tested at distance.

problem: A model reports near-perfect scores on a public benchmark whose test items predate the model's training cutoff. A draft: 'state-of-the-art capability — cite the score as evidence of true skill.' Evaluate and name the checks.
thinking: Structural risk: benchmark items available before the cutoff can appear in pretraining corpora — memorization/contamination produces scores that measure recall, not capability.
First invalid step: 'predate cutoff → clean' — it is the reverse: pre-cutoff items are the CONTAMINATION-EXPOSED ones; genuinely held-out evaluation requires post-cutoff or controlled items.

Detection toolkit: (a) perturb items (rename entities, change numbers) — a large score drop suggests memorized templates; (b) probe with masked or reordered variants of test items; (c) n-gram/overlap scans between the test set and public corpora; (d) items written post-cutoff, or a private holdout.
Predictions that discriminate: true skill → similar scores on perturbed and fresh items; contamination → big drops on perturbation and on fresh items.
Check the claim's support base: a single pre-cutoff benchmark number can't carry 'state of the art' at all — triangulate with post-cutoff benchmarks and out-of-distribution evaluations.
reference_answer:
Pre-cutoff public benchmarks are contamination-prone: run perturbation probes (should preserve skill, collapse memorization), overlap scans, and favor post-cutoff/private holdouts. The score alone can't distinguish capability from recall — 'cite as evidence' is premature.

**Answer:** contamination risk unexamined; perturbation + fresh-holdout evidence required before the skill claim.
failure_modes: score as capability without leak audit

problem: A 60-year-old woman carries the family's pathogenic BRCA1 variant; her mother had breast cancer at 45, but she has had none. Her daughter asks: 'Does that mean the variant is harmless?' Answer carefully.
thinking: Penetrance for a dominant cancer-predisposition variant is age-dependent and modified by other genes and environment, so it cannot be read off two relatives — and harmless is not on the table of possible readings.

For a BRCA1 pathogenic variant the lifetime risk is high but incomplete, accruing across decades: a carrier who is cancer-free at 60 has a lower residual risk than she did at birth, but not zero, and her mother's early cancer pulls the family history, and the risk model, in the other direction.

The daughter's question maps onto her own status: if she carries the same variant, her risk follows from the variant classification and gene-specific age-dependent curves, refined by family history and screening guidance; if she does not, the inherited risk disappears — which is why testing her is actionable rather than theoretical.

Uncertainty about individual modifiers remains, and the practical answer is counselling and screening according to guidelines, which works precisely because the risk is real but not certain. So: no — reduced observed events don't make the variant harmless; risk stays individual, age-dependent, and partly uncertain — counsel and screen. The pattern: penetrance is a population probability by age, not a coin flip per family.
reference_answer:
No. Penetrance for a BRCA1 pathogenic variant is **age-dependent** (risk accrues across decades) and modified by other genetic and environmental factors, so two women in one family don't define a personal probability. Her mother's early cancer and her own clean history change her residual risk estimate modestly — they don't make the variant harmless, and if her daughter carries the same variant she has her own elevated, age-dependent risk. The actionable response is genetic counseling with age-adjusted risk models and adherence to high-risk screening, which works precisely because the risk is real but not certain.

**Answer:** no — reduced observed events don't make the variant harmless; risk stays individual, age-dependent, and partly uncertain — counsel and screen.

problem: Two beakers: 0.1 M HCl and 0.1 M acetic acid. A draft says 'same concentration, so equal conductivity.' Compare and explain.
thinking: Conductivity tracks free ions, so equal nominal concentrations say nothing until the degree of dissociation of each acid is known.
HCl dissociates completely: [H⁺] ≈ 0.1 M. Acetic acid dissociates only slightly: [H⁺] ≈ √(Ka·C) = √(1.8 × 10⁻⁵ × 0.1) ≈ 1.3 × 10⁻³ M — roughly 75 times fewer charge carriers.
The pH gap is the direct indicator the draft ignored: HCl sits near pH 1 and acetic acid near pH 2.9, and the difference in pH mirrors the difference in H⁺ concentrations.
So: HCl conducts much more — equal molarity, very different dissociation. The pattern: equal formal concentration does not mean equal ion concentration.
reference_answer:
Not equal: conductivity tracks **free ions**, so 0.1 M HCl (fully dissociated, ~0.1 M H₃O⁺) conducts far better than 0.1 M acetic acid (≈1.3×10⁻³ M H₃O⁺, about 1% dissociated). The pH gap (≈1 vs ≈2.9) is the direct indicator the draft ignored by equating nominal concentrations.

**Answer:** HCl conducts much more — equal molarity, very different dissociation.
verification: compare pH values as a proxy for free H+
failure_modes: formal concentration equated with ion concentration

problem: Detect whether a singly linked list contains a cycle. A draft stores visited nodes in a set and claims its solution is 'optimal in both time and space.' Evaluate and give the optimal-space algorithm.
thinking: The visited-set method is correct but uses O(n) extra space, so calling it space-optimal is false.
1. Floyd's tortoise and hare detects a cycle in O(n) time and O(1) space.
2. Slow moves 1 step and fast moves 2; inside a cycle the gap closes by 1 per step, so they must meet; if fast reaches None there is no cycle.
3. Edge cases: empty list, and a single node pointing to itself.
4. Check: an acyclic five-node list never meets, and a list with a tail entering a cycle meets.
5. General pattern: claiming optimality needs a comparison with known alternatives.
reference_answer:
Correct but not space-optimal: the set costs O(n). Floyd's algorithm does O(n) time, O(1) space:

```python
def has_cycle(head):
    slow = fast = head
    while fast and fast.next:
        slow = slow.next
        fast = fast.next.next
        if slow is fast:
            return True
    return False
```

Meeting proof: inside the cycle the gap shrinks by 1 per step, so they must coincide; fast hitting None proves acyclicity. Edge cases: empty list, one self-looping node.

**Answer:** use Floyd's two-pointer method — O(n) time, O(1) space; the draft's 'optimal in space' claim is false.
ground_truth: Floyd O(n)/O(1); set method O(n) space
verification: run both on cyclic/acyclic cases; gap-closing argument

problem: Find all integer solutions of $x^2 - 4y^2 = 16$.
thinking: Factor first: (x − 2y)(x + 2y) = 16. The factors are congruent to x modulo 2, so they share the parity of x and, with an even product, both are even — but a second condition also appears: their difference is 4y.
With a = x − 2y and b = x + 2y, the back-substitution is x = (a + b)/2 and y = (b − a)/4, so integrality requires b − a ≡ 0 (mod 4).
Checking the even factor pairs: (2, 8), (8, 2), (−2, −8) and (−8, −2) all give b − a = ±6 and fail, while (4, 4) gives b − a = 0 with (x, y) = (4, 0), and (−4, −4) gives the mirror (−4, 0).

So (x, y) = (4, 0) or (−4, 0), and the check is immediate: 16 − 0 = 16 ✓ for both, while (2, 8) would force y = 3/2, not an integer. The pattern: when y carries a coefficient inside the factored squares, the factor pairs must also satisfy the divisibility of the difference — and that extra condition is where the spurious candidates die.
reference_answer:
Factor: $(x-2y)(x+2y) = 16$. Since $x \pm 2y \equiv x \pmod 2$, the two factors have the same parity — always even here. Writing $a = x-2y$, $b = x+2y$: $x = (a+b)/2$ and $y = (b-a)/4$, so integrality needs $b - a \equiv 0 \pmod 4$. Among even factor pairs: $(2,8), (8,2), (-2,-8), (-8,-2)$ give $b-a = \pm 6$ ✗; $(4,4)$ gives $(4,0)$ and $(-4,-4)$ gives $(-4,0)$ ✓. Check: $4^2 - 4\cdot 0^2 = 16$ ✓.

**Answer:** $(x, y) = (4, 0)$ or $(-4, 0)$

problem: A worker pool shuts down by having EACH producer put a sentinel None on the queue; consumers exit when they see None. With three producers and two consumers, the pipeline sometimes exits early and sometimes never terminates, and messages vanish. A draft: 'one sentinel per producer is exactly the right count.' Diagnose.
thinking: Failure mode 1 (early exit): consumers treat ANY None as shutdown — with three sentinels and two consumers, a consumer that sees the FIRST None quits while other producers are still sending; remaining messages (and later sentinels) sit unconsumed → lost work and mis-shutdown.

Failure mode 2 (never terminates / hang): sentinels interleave with real messages — a consumer can consume a None placed mid-stream as its shutdown while its sibling consumes messages + a second None and exits, leaving the THIRD sentinel (and any post-sentinel messages) in the queue with nobody alive to drain; producer-side join() then blocks forever.

First invalid step: 'one per producer = right count' — sentinels are channel markers, not per-producer tokens; the accounting must be per-CONSUMER exit condition, not per-PRODUCER count, and ordering matters: none may precede any producer's last message.

Correct patterns: (a) producers send sentinels only AFTER their last real message, and consumers exit after consuming N_PRODUCERS sentinels collectively (count them, shared under a lock/Counter); (b) better: sentinel is not the mechanism — close the queue (queue.shutdown() in modern APIs) or use an explicit 'producers done' event JOINed before putting one sentinel, or a completion barrier; (c) task_done()/join() for backlog accounting so exit cannot precede drained work.

Verification: stress test with producers of unequal speed and a message AFTER one producer's sentinel — the early-exit and hang both reproduce deterministically under a scheduler that interleaves sends and gets.
Check the draft's premise with two producers/one consumer: even then, sentinel N before producer 2's last message causes early exit — the count was never the real invariant.
reference_answer:
Sentinel counting is the wrong invariant: with interleaving, a consumer sees the first None and exits while producers still send (lost messages), later sentinels pile up with no consumer (hang at join). Fix by making shutdown a completion event — queue.close(), or join producers first then signal once, counting exits per consumer — with ordering: sentinel strictly after every producer's final message. Stress with unequal producers to reproduce.

**Answer:** per-producer sentinels + multiple consumers race on both ends; use a close/completion mechanism with per-consumer accounting and order guarantees.
ground_truth: early-exit and hang races; use close/join-first signaling
verification: unequal-speed stress test reproduces both failures

problem: In a day, Alice can make 2 cakes or 4 pies; Bob can make 1 cake or 3 pies. A draft: 'Bob is worse at both — no gains from trade are possible.' Evaluate.
thinking: Opportunity costs: Alice: 1 cake costs 2 pies (or 0.5 cakes per pie); Bob: 1 cake costs 3 pies (or 1/3 cake per pie).
Comparative advantage: Bob gives up LESS for a pie (1/3 < 1/2) → Bob should specialize in pies; Alice gives up less for a cake (2 < 3) → Alice in cakes.

First invalid step: absolute-advantage framing — 'worse at both' describes productivity levels, but gains from trade are governed by RELATIVE costs; Bob's pies are comparatively cheap for the same reason his cakes are comparatively dear.

Check gains: with trade at, say, 1 cake ↔ 2.5 pies: Alice sells a cake for 2.5 (better than 2), buys pies at 2.5 (worse than her 2)? — pick the exchange to confirm both gain: Alice values a cake at 2 pies, Bob at 3 — any price in (2, 3) makes both better ✓ e.g., 2.5.

Consumption check at 2.5 pies per cake: Alice sells one cake — keeps 1 cake + 2.5 pies, which beats her own frontier (1 cake + 2 pies alone); Bob sells 2.5 pies — keeps 0.5 pies + 1 cake, impossible alone (a full day makes him 1 cake OR 3 pies) ✓ both outside autarky.
reference_answer:
Comparative costs: pies cost Bob 1/3 cake vs Alice 1/2 → Bob specializes in pies, Alice in cakes; any cake-price in (2, 3) pies leaves both better. The draft confused absolute productivity with relative cost.

**Answer:** gains exist — Alice cakes, Bob pies; 'worse at both' doesn't preclude comparative advantage.
ground_truth: Alice cakes, Bob pies; gains possible

problem: Five runners finish a race. Clues: A finishes before B; B before C; C before E; D is unconstrained. A draft: 'E must finish last, since C beats E and everything else is ordered.' Determine who can be last.
thinking: From the clues: A < B < C < E (a strict chain); D floats anywhere.
Construct two valid orders: A B C D E (E last) and A B C E D (D last) — positions of D and E are interchangeable in the tail.
First invalid step: 'E must be last' — C < E orders E after C only; it says nothing about D, and D placed after E satisfies every clue.
So the sharp answer: last is D or E (both possible); A, B, C can never be last.
Check E-last case: A B C D E → every clue holds ✓; D-last: A B C E D → ✓. Two feasible orders, two possible last places.
reference_answer:
The chain is A<B<C<E with D free: valid orders include A B C D E and A B C E D → last ∈ {D, E}. The draft turned an ordering into a uniqueness claim — 'must' needs the absence of alternatives, and D provides one.

**Answer:** D or E can be last (C, B, A cannot); E-last is possible, not necessary.

problem: Two services feed the same dashboard: one emits naive datetimes (documented as 'UTC internally'), one emits timezone-aware datetimes. A draft says 'comparisons and sorting will work — both are datetimes.' Evaluate in Python.
thinking: We need the comparison contract: Python forbids ordering naive and aware datetimes — comparing them raises TypeError (you can't order a time without a zone against one with).
So the dashboard's sort raises the first time the two streams interleave — the draft's 'both are datetimes' describes the type, not the comparability.
First invalid step: structural typing ('both datetime instances') treated as semantic compatibility — the naive/aware distinction is exactly the attribute the operation requires.

Fix: normalize at ingest — convert the naive stream to aware (attach timezone.utc, per its documented convention) or convert both to UTC epochs; enforce one representation at the boundary with a validator so mixed streams can't re-enter.
Verify: sorted([naive, aware]) raises TypeError today; after normalization, ordering proceeds and equals the epoch-order sanity check.
Self-check the equality corner: == between naive and aware returns False (no exception) — so equality bugs slip through while ordering crashes; both behaviors flow from the same frame mismatch.
Self-reflection: 'same class' is the weakest compatibility claim — check the operators the pipeline actually uses (order, subtract, compare) against the class's documented rules.
Conclusion: normalize to one aware representation at ingest.
reference_answer:
Naive vs aware comparison raises TypeError (ordering) — 'both are datetimes' isn't comparability. Fix: normalize at ingest (attach timezone.utc to the naive stream per its documented convention, or convert both to epoch); validate at the boundary. Note == returns False silently — same mismatch, quieter failure.

**Answer:** not comparable — normalize representations before mixing.

problem: A company applies a new coaching program to its 5 lowest-performing stores; next quarter all 5 improve. A draft concludes 'the program works — the worst stores jumped.' Evaluate and design the valid test.
thinking: Choosing the five lowest performers selects an extreme, and extremes partly reflect luck that reverts.
1. Regression to the mean predicts improvement for the selected stores even if the program does nothing.
2. The draft has no counterfactual: it compared the stores with their own extreme baseline.
3. Valid test: randomly assign half of the eligible low performers to coaching and half to delayed or no coaching, and compare the changes between the arms.
4. If both arms improve similarly, the program adds nothing; a sustained differential improvement would support it.
5. General pattern: treating the worst group always starts from a dip, so use randomisation.
reference_answer:
Selecting the worst stores builds in reversion: they improve even with a null program, so 'all 5 improved' is uninformative. Valid test: randomly assign eligible low performers to coaching vs control (or stagger), then compare CHANGES between arms — effect = differential improvement. Falsifier: similar improvements in both arms ⇒ no program effect.

**Answer:** invalid as run (regression to the mean); randomize among low performers and compare change differences.
verification: state the null-program prediction; check design against it

problem: Five positive numbers have mean 10. A draft: 'their median cannot exceed 10 — the middle value is dragged down by whatever balances the average.' Evaluate with a construction or refutation.
thinking: Build a concrete example: {4, 8, 12, 13, 13}: sum 50 → mean 10 ✓; sorted middle = 12 → median 12 > mean 10 ✓.

First invalid step: 'the median is dragged down' — no law forces median ≤ mean; skew's direction decides: a heavy LEFT tail (a few small values) pulls the mean below the median, exactly the construction above.
The supposed 'drag' argument confuses two different statistics: balancing the sum constrains the TOTAL, not the middle position.
Check the mirror case to cement the principle: {7, 7, 8, 8, 20} → mean 10, median 8 < mean (right tail pulls mean up) ✓ both directions possible.
reference_answer:
Refuted: {4, 8, 12, 13, 13} gives mean 10, median 12. Skew direction moves mean and median apart in either order; the draft asserted a constraint that doesn't exist.

**Answer:** possible — median can exceed the mean (e.g., 4, 8, 12, 13, 13).
verification: sum/median computed for both example and mirror case

problem: How many ONTO functions map a 3-element set to a 2-element set? A draft answers 2³ = 8. Evaluate.
thinking: We need surjections: every codomain element hit — subtract the non-onto functions from all functions.
All functions: 2³ = 8. Non-onto: functions missing at least one codomain element — i.e., CONSTANT functions (all three inputs to one output): 2 of them.
First invalid step: the draft counted all functions; 'onto' is a constraint the count must enforce, and the constants are exactly the violators here.

Verify by listing with domain {a,b,c}, codomain {0,1}: onto functions must contain both outputs; count by which output is the singleton image: output-0 used once (3 choices of input) or output-1 used once (3) → 6 ✓.
Inclusion–exclusion cross-check: Σ(−1)^k C(2,k)(2−k)³ = 2³ − 2·1³ = 6 ✓.
Self-check the general shape: onto from 3 to 2 is C(2,1)... the formula 2!·S(3,2) = 2 × 3 = 6 ✓ (Stirling) — three routes agree.
Conclusion: 6.
reference_answer:
Surjections = 2³ − 2 = **6** (drop the two constant functions); verified by singleton-output counting (3+3) and by Stirling 2!·S(3,2) = 6 ✓. The draft counted all functions; 'onto' excludes the constants.

**Answer:** 6.

problem: Design a complete brand identity for the website of a specialty coffee roastery called Ember & Oak. It sells single-origin beans in small batches, roasts on-site, and wants to feel like a slow, warm, hand-crafted workshop rather than a tech-forward coffee startup. Deliver the identity system: positioning, palette with exact hex values and accessibility reasoning, typography with a modular scale, layout and spacing foundations, key components, a logo concept, motion rules, and voice.
thinking: Start from positioning, because every color and type decision has to answer to it. The brief says slow, warm, hand-crafted workshop; the audience is people who buy beans by origin and brew at home with intent. That rules out the cold minimal-white aesthetic of tech coffee apps and also rules out rustic overload (kraft paper everywhere reads as farmers-market cheap, not premium craft). The identity has to sit between editorial and tactile.

Explore three directions. Direction A, Gilded Espresso: near-black backgrounds, gold foil accents, thin serif. Rejected because dark-heavy pages make origin stories and brew guides feel inaccessible and the gold accent fails contrast on the cream surfaces the client wants for long-form content. Direction B, Paper Ledger: cream backgrounds, one ink color, tiny typographic details, stamp-like mark. This is the chosen foundation because it reads as a workshop notebook: calm, tactile, trustworthy, and it makes photography of beans and crema the loudest element on the page. Direction C, Retro Roaster: 70s packaging palette with mustard and rust. Rejected as too costume-like; it would date quickly and fight the premium price point.

Palette, derived and checked. Background cream #F6EFE4 (paper, warm but not yellow). Primary ink #2A1E16 (roasted bean brown, near-black): contrast on cream is 14.19:1, well past AAA for body text at any size. Muted text #6B5A4A at 5.77:1 on cream passes AA for body copy, used for captions, metadata, brew tables. Ember accent #B4552D (the brand's signature burnt orange): 4.30:1 on cream, which is below the 4.5:1 body threshold, so the rule is explicit: ember is allowed only for text at 24px and larger, for icons, rules, and illustration fills. Primary buttons are ember with #FFFFFF text at 4.91:1, passing AA. For small links and any text under 24px that must be ember-toned, the deeper mix #8F3F1F is used at 6.34:1 on cream. This gives the design a disciplined two-tier accent system instead of a single color used carelessly everywhere.

Typography. Display: a high-contrast serif with soft terminals (Fraunces or similar) for headings, origin names, and pull quotes; it carries the editorial workshop voice. Text and UI: a neutral grotesk (Inter or similar) for body, tables, and controls, because brew guides include numbers and the UI must stay crisp. Modular scale ratio 1.25 anchored at 16px base gives steps 16, 20, 25, 31, 39; body sits at 16-20, section headings at 25-31, hero display at 39 and up with optical letter-spacing tightened to -0.01em. Line height 1.5 for body, 1.15 for display. Never italic for UI labels; italics are reserved for origin tasting notes.

Layout and spacing. 12-column grid, 24px gutters, 1200px max content width, single column under 768px. Spacing rhythm on a 4pt base with an 8pt feel: 4, 8, 12, 16, 24, 32, 48, 64. Cards use 1px hairlines in a tan mix (#E4D8C6) rather than shadows, to keep the ledger feel; shadows appear only on the cart drawer (0 8px 24px rgba(42,30,22,0.12)). Radius is 4px on inputs, 8px on cards, full pill only for the roast-level tag.

Components and states. Primary button (ember bg, white label, 44px min height, hover darkens to #8F3F1F, active scales 0.98, focus-visible ring 2px #2A1E16 with 2px offset). Secondary button is a 1.5px ink outline with transparent fill. Product card shows origin, process, roast level tag, price; the tag color encodes roast level (light #D9A066, medium #B4552D, dark #6B4A32) always paired with a text label so color is never the only signal. Forms use 44px targets, labels above inputs, errors in a red that must be checked separately against cream (use 4.5:1 minimum).

Logo concept. A monogram mark: a lowercase ampersand where the upper bowl becomes a rising flame and the lower bowl a bean silhouette, drawn on a 24px grid with 2px strokes so it survives at favicon size. Wordmark: Fraunces semibold, letter-spacing 0.02em, set beside the mark; stacked lockup for packaging. Keep the mark one color (ink or cream inverse) so it never fights photography.

Motion. 150-250ms, ease-out for entrances, ease-in-out for state changes; no parallax over text; hover lifts translate 2px only. Respect prefers-reduced-motion by replacing transitions with instant states. Page-load sequence: logo mark draws stroke-first, then content fades in 120ms staggered by 40ms, capped at 6 items.

Voice. Calm expert: short declarative sentences, sensory but precise tasting notes, no hype adjectives, no emoji. Microcopy example: instead of a generic empty cart message, the cart says the roast schedule and when the next batch ships.

Accessibility audit summary: body ink pair 14.19:1; muted 5.77:1; ember restricted to 24px+ (4.30:1) and ember buttons with white text (4.91:1); deep ember for small links 6.34:1; roast-level tags always carry text labels; focus rings present on every interactive element; tap targets 44px minimum.
reference_answer:
Identity system for Ember & Oak (slow-craft roastery):
Palette tokens - Ink #2A1E16 (text, 14.19:1 on cream), Cream #F6EFE4 (background), Muted #6B5A4A (secondary text, 5.77:1), Ember #B4552D (primary accent; 4.30:1 on cream so only for 24px+ text, icons, rules, and buttons whose white labels measure 4.91:1), Deep Ember #8F3F1F (small links, 6.34:1), Hairline #E4D8C6.
Type - display serif (Fraunces-class) for headings, neutral grotesk (Inter-class) for UI; scale 1.25 from 16px: 16/20/25/31/39; line-height 1.5 body, 1.15 display.
Layout - 12-col grid, 24px gutters, 1200px max, 4/8/12/16/24/32/48/64 spacing, hairline cards, radius 4-8px.
Logo - ampersand monogram whose bowls form a flame and a bean, 24px grid, 2px strokes, one-color lockups; wordmark in the display serif.
Voice - calm expert, sensory precision, no hype.
Accessibility - every body pair >= 4.5:1 verified; ember two-tier rule (large text/icons vs deep ember for small text); roast-level color tags always labeled in text.

problem: Can a standard 8×8 chessboard with two diagonally OPPOSITE corners removed (62 squares) be tiled by 1×2 dominoes? A draft: '62 squares is even, so yes — dominoes cover 2 squares each.'
thinking: Count parity is necessary, not sufficient — tileability needs the stronger coloring invariant.
Checkerboard coloring: 32 black, 32 white. Opposite corners share a color → after removal: 30 of one color, 32 of the other.
Every domino covers exactly one black and one white — k dominoes cover k of each, so a tiled region MUST have equal color counts. 30 ≠ 32 → impossible.
First invalid step: the draft's test used only the total (even), discarding the per-color ledger that the domino's structure enforces.

Contrast to pin the principle: removing two ADJACENT (opposite-colored) corners leaves 31–31 — even count AND balanced colors — and that board (plus a minor geometric argument) can be tiled; the invariant that decides is coloring, not parity.
reference_answer:
Impossible: opposite corners are same-colored, leaving 30/32 — dominoes must place one square on each color, requiring equality. Even square count was the draft's weaker (necessary-only) test.

**Answer:** no tiling — 30/32 color imbalance; parity of the count is necessary but not sufficient.

problem: Educational vignette: a patient asks whether to take a preventive medicine. Their 10-year risk of the outcome is 1.0% without it and 0.8% with it. A draft: 'yes — a 20% reduction is substantial.' Evaluate the decision support.
thinking: We need the absolute frame: the relative 20% (1.0 → 0.8) is an absolute reduction of 0.2 percentage points over TEN years — NNT ≈ 500 (1/0.002) to prevent one event over that horizon.

First invalid step: presenting only the relative figure and prescribing — '20%' sounds large; '2 in 1,000 to 1.6 in 1,000, so ~500 treated for one event avoided over 10 years' is the honest scale; the draft chose the framing that maximizes the sell.

The decision's other pan: harms, burdens, and costs of the medicine (side effects, monitoring) — absent entirely; a ~0.2% absolute benefit is exactly the territory where preference sensitivity peaks (guideline bodies flag small-absolute-benefit decisions as preference-sensitive).

Correct support: give BOTH frames (absolute events avoided + relative), name the NNT and the horizon, list common/rare harms, and hand the decision to the patient's values — 'some will take it for the small chance; many will decline to avoid the burden' is the accurate summary.

Self-check against the reverse error: blanket 'decline — tiny benefit' would commit the mirror sin (deciding FOR the patient what weight to put on a small absolute gain) — the point is framing, not a mandate.
Verification frame: teach-back — can the patient restate 'about 500 treated, 1 event avoided over 10 years'? Comprehension is the endpoint, not the prescription.
Self-reflection: relative reductions inflate small bases — decision quality starts with the base rate on the table.
Conclusion: present absolute + relative + harms; preference-sensitive; no verdict from the draft's framing.
reference_answer:
Frame check: 20% relative = 0.2 percentage points absolute over 10 years (NNT ≈ 500). Harm profile and burdens unstated; small-absolute-benefit decisions are preference-sensitive. Correct support: both frames + harms + patient's values; teach-back restatement (≈1 in 500 over 10 years) as the comprehension endpoint. The draft sold the relative figure and decided for the patient.

**Answer:** biased framing — present absolute terms, harms, and a values-based choice.

problem: A draft claims: 'every change in the DNA base sequence changes the protein produced.' Evaluate and give a concrete counterexample.
thinking: The genetic code is degenerate — several codons encode the same amino acid — so some base changes leave the protein untouched.
The concrete counterexample: GGU and GGC both encode glycine, so a third-position change between them is a silent (synonymous) substitution and the protein is identical.

The claim fails on that single case, and broader classes exist too: changes in non-coding regions can leave the protein unchanged, as can substitutions that preserve the amino acid through another codon.
So: claim false — synonymous (silent) substitutions exist, e.g. GGU → GGC (both glycine). The pattern: a counterexample to every needs only one specific case, and degeneracy supplies it immediately.
reference_answer:
False: the code is degenerate, so many substitutions are **silent**. GGU and GGC both encode glycine — a third-base change there leaves the protein identical. Substitutions outside coding or regulatory regions similarly may change nothing. Some changes alter function subtly or not at all; 'every change matters' is not how the code works.

**Answer:** claim false — synonymous (silent) substitutions exist, e.g. GGU → GGC (both glycine).
verification: substitute the third base of a glycine codon

problem: User-supplied IDs are validated with the regex `^(a+)+$`. Request times blow up exponentially as ID length grows. A draft: 'regex matching is linear in input size — the slowdown must be the network.' Diagnose.
thinking: Pattern analysis: nested quantifier (a+)+ — for a string of n a's followed by a failing character, the engine (backtracking family) tries every way to partition the a's between the inner and outer repeats: ~2^(n−1) paths before declaring failure.

First invalid step: 'regex is linear' — that's true for DFA-style engines and for patterns WITHOUT ambiguity; backtracking engines can go exponential on nested quantifiers over the same character class.
Empirical shape: doubling input length roughly DOUBLES the time per added character (×2 per char) — measure and it prints as exponential, not the linear slope the draft assumed.

Fixes: rewrite to a non-ambiguous equivalent (a+ alone suffices for THIS intent); or use possessive/atomic quantifiers if supported; or bound input length and add timeouts; or switch to an RE2-style linear engine.
Check the intent: ^(a+)+$ and ^a+$ accept exactly the same strings — the nesting buys nothing and only opens the blow-up.
reference_answer:
Catastrophic backtracking: (a+)+ partitions each run of a's 2ⁿ ways on failure paths. Rewrite to ^a+$ (equivalent language), or use atomic/possessive groups, length caps/timeouts, or a linear-time engine. The draft's 'linear' claim omits the engine's backtracking model.

**Answer:** exponential on adversarial input — denest the quantifier; measure doubling per character to confirm.

problem: For which real m does x² + mx + 9 = 0 have two distinct real roots? A draft answers m > 6. Evaluate completeness.
thinking: We need discriminant > 0: m² − 36 > 0 → |m| > 6.
First invalid step: the draft solved half the inequality — m² − 36 > 0 gives m > 6 OR m < −6; only the positive branch was reported.
Branch check by example: m = −10 → x² − 10x + 9 = 0 → roots 1 and 9, two distinct reals ✓ — the excluded branch is full of valid cases.
Boundary audit: m = 6 → x² + 6x + 9 = (x+3)² — one repeated root ✗; m = −6 → (x−3)² same ✗ — so the endpoints are correctly excluded and the set is open on both sides.
Symmetry intuition for why both branches must appear: the quadratic's constant term is +9 and only the linear coefficient's MAGNITUDE matters to the discriminant — the discriminator is even in m.
Self-check the answer format: 'm > 6 or m < −6' (equivalently |m| > 6) ✓ complete.
Conclusion: |m| > 6.
reference_answer:
Discriminant: m² > 36 → **|m| > 6** (m > 6 or m < −6). Check: m = −10 gives roots 1, 9 ✓; m = ±6 give double roots (excluded). The draft kept one branch; the discriminant is even in m, so both signs survive.

**Answer:** m < −6 or m > 6.

problem: Show that n² + 3n + 2 is even for every integer n. A draft 'proves' it by checking n = 0, 1, 2, 3, 4. Evaluate the proof.
thinking: A finite list of examples cannot prove a statement about every integer: checking n = 0 through 4 says nothing about the untested n, so the draft's method is not a proof regardless of whether the claim is true.
The valid route by factoring: n² + 3n + 2 = (n + 1)(n + 2), a product of two consecutive integers, one of which is even — so the product is even for every n.
The parity route agrees, case by case: n even gives even + even + even; n odd gives odd + odd + even = even.

The tested values (2, 6, 12, 20, 30) are consistent with the claim but carry no proof weight. So: the claim is true, but the draft's check of five values is not a proof — use the parity cases or the consecutive-integer factorization. The pattern: examples make a for-all claim plausible, and only a covering argument establishes it.
reference_answer:
The example-check is not a proof: it says nothing about untested n. The valid arguments: (a) parity cases — n even gives even + even + even; n odd gives odd + odd + even = even; or (b) factor as (n+1)(n+2), a product of consecutive integers, always even. Note the final claim is true — the defect is the reasoning, and the fact is confirmed by both correct routes.

**Answer:** the claim is true, but the draft's check of five values is not a proof — use the parity cases or the consecutive-integer factorization.

problem: Six rolls of a fair die: P(exactly two sixes)? A draft answers (1/6)² = 1/36 ≈ 2.8%. Evaluate.
thinking: We need the binomial term: C(6,2)(1/6)²(5/6)⁴.
First invalid step: the draft keeps only the two successes' factor — dropping BOTH the four non-six outcomes (5/6)⁴ AND the position factor C(6,2). Both omissions shrink the probability drastically.

Structural check of magnitude: two sixes in six is the MODE of the binomial (np ≈ 1): its probability should be substantial (~0.2); the draft's 2.8% describes something closer to six-specific positioning.
Verify against the full distribution: P(0)=0.335, P(1)=0.402, P(2)=0.201, P(3)=0.054 — summing the listed ≈ 0.99 with the tail ✓ the 0.201 sits correctly as the peak region.
Self-check the position factor: 15 placements of which two rolls are sixes — the same event set counted multiply, hence the multiplier.
Conclusion: ≈ 0.201.
reference_answer:
Binomial: C(6,2)(1/6)²(5/6)⁴ = 15×625/46656 ≈ **0.201**. The draft kept only the successes' factor — no position count, no failure factors; distribution check (0.335/0.402/0.201/0.054) places the mode correctly at 1–2 sixes.

**Answer:** ≈ 0.20.

problem: A 0.5 kg ball is released from rest 2 m above sand and sinks 5 cm before stopping. (a) Average resistance force from the sand? A draft: 'F = mgh/d = 0.5·10·2/0.05 = 200 N.' (b) If the sink depth were only 3 cm, would the average resistance stay under a 150 N design limit?
thinking: Energy accounting: the ball falls 2 m freely and then 5 cm more while decelerating — total drop 2.05 m; all of mg(2.05) is absorbed over the stopping distance d = 0.05 m.

First invalid step in the draft: using h only — the sink distance itself adds to the fall, the classic (h + d)/d subtlety; the error is small here (205 vs 200) precisely because d is small, which is why it hides.
Part (b): F = 0.5·10·2.03/0.03 ≈ 338 N — the shallower stop is LESS compliant: same energy absorbed over a shorter distance → force up, far exceeding 150 N.
Check the trend direction: d → 0⁺ ⇒ F → ∞ — stopping harder always means larger force; 338 > 205 > 150 ✓ consistent ordering.
reference_answer:
F = mg(h+d)/d = 205 N (draft's 200 N omits the extra d in the numerator). For d = 3 cm: 338 N ≫ 150 N — the shallower sand violates the design limit; stopping distance sets the force, inversely.

**Answer:** (a) ≈ 205 N; (b) no — 338 N exceeds the 150 N limit.
verification: full drop height (h+d) + d→0 limit trend

problem: A frictionless banked curve: radius 100 m, design speed 20 m/s (g = 9.8). Find the banking angle. A draft answers θ = v²/(rg) = 0.408°. Evaluate.
thinking: We need the geometry: the required tilt satisfies tan θ = v²/(rg) — a RATIO of accelerations, not the angle itself.
Angle: θ = arctan(0.408) ≈ 22.2°.

First invalid step: reporting the tangent's value as degrees — 0.408° would mean an almost flat curve; the missing arctan is the whole error (and the units '°' don't fit a dimensionless ratio without the trig.)

Sanity check: at 20 m/s ≈ 72 km/h on a 100 m radius, the tires' requirement is about 0.4 g of lateral force — needing a bank of ~22° matches driving intuition for such a curve; 0.4° would be a barely-tilted track unable to help.

Verify the limit: if θ → 0, tan θ → 0 forces v → 0 (flat road needs speed zero without friction) — with 0.408° the 'design speed' would be √(rg·0.00712) ≈ 2.6 m/s, contradicting the stated 20 m/s ✓ the draft's angle fails its own design speed.
Self-reflection: trig inverses are the standard omission after solving for a ratio — label each quantity (ratio vs angle) before answering.
Conclusion: ≈ 22.2°.
reference_answer:
tan θ = v²/(rg) = 0.408 → θ = arctan(0.408) ≈ **22.2°**. The draft mistook the ratio for the angle (0.408°); check: its angle gives design speed ≈2.6 m/s, contradicting the stated 20 m/s. Inverses convert ratios to angles.

**Answer:** ≈ 22.2°.

problem: In how many orderings of 5 distinct books does book A come before book B? A draft reasons: 'fix A in position 1 (4! ways), then position 2 (24)... multiply by positions: 24 × 5 = 120.' Evaluate.
thinking: We need the count where A precedes B in the order.
Symmetry: in every ordering exactly one of A-before-B or B-before-A holds, and the pairing is a bijection (swap A and B) → exactly half the orderings: 5!/2 = 60.

First invalid step: the draft's position-fixing counts A's placements but pairs each with ALL arrangements of the rest — overcounting the constraint's effect; its 120 exceeds half of 120 (the total), an internal absurdity.

Verify the draft's arithmetic differently: position 1 for A: 24 ways ✓; position 2: 24; ... position 5: 24 — that sums to 120 = 5! — the count with NO constraint at all (B free to be anywhere, including before A) — the constraint did nothing in the draft's method.

Independent check by direct summation with constraint: A in position k → B must be in one of the k−1 positions after? no — B among the remaining 4 slots AFTER k? Sum over A=k of (positions for B after) — simplest is the symmetry argument; also direct: choose 2 slots for {A,B} (C(5,2) = 10), A first in each (1 way), others 3! → 10 × 6 = 60 ✓ two routes agree.
Self-check the half-argument's validity: no ordering has A = B (distinct books) → the two cases partition → half ✓.
Conclusion: 60.
reference_answer:
5!/2 = **60**: the swap-A↔B bijection pairs the two cases, partitioning all 120 orderings in half. Direct route: C(5,2) slots for the pair × 3! = 60 ✓. The draft's method counted all 120 orderings — the constraint never entered its arithmetic.

**Answer:** 60.
failure_modes: constraint does no work in method

problem: Find all integers $n$ such that $n^4 + 4$ is prime.
thinking: n⁴ + 4 looks prime-friendly, but it carries a hidden factorization — the Sophie Germain identity: n⁴ + 4 = (n² − 2n + 2)(n² + 2n + 2).
The expansion confirms it: (n² − 2n + 2)(n² + 2n + 2) = n⁴ + 2n³ + 2n² − 2n³ − 4n² − 4n + 2n² + 4n + 4 = n⁴ + 4 ✓.
Both factors are positive, so n⁴ + 4 is prime only if one factor equals 1: n² − 2n + 2 = 1 means (n − 1)² = 0, giving n = 1, and n² + 2n + 2 = 1 means (n + 1)² = 0, giving n = −1.

Both give 5, which is prime, while for |n| ≥ 2 both factors are at least 2 and the number is composite — n = 3 gives 85 = 5 × 17 ✓ and n = 0 gives 4. So the solutions are n = ±1. The pattern: n⁴ + 4, and more generally n⁴ + 4m⁴, factors after adding and subtracting a middle term to form a difference of squares.
reference_answer:
Apply the Sophie Germain identity:

$$n^4+4 = (n^2-2n+2)(n^2+2n+2)$$

(expand: $n^4+2n^3+2n^2-2n^3-4n^2-4n+2n^2+4n+4 = n^4+4$ ✓). Both factors are positive, so $n^4+4$ is prime exactly when one of them is 1:

- $n^2-2n+2 = 1 \iff (n-1)^2 = 0 \iff n = 1$;
- $n^2+2n+2 = 1 \iff (n+1)^2 = 0 \iff n = -1$.

Both give $5$, prime. For $|n| \ge 2$, both factors are at least 2, so the number is composite. Check: $n = 3$: $85 = 5\cdot 17$ ✓.

**Answer:** $n = \pm 1$

problem: USER asks for 'the exact URL of the WHO page listing all approved malaria vaccines.' A draft replies: 'https://www.who.int/vaccines/malaria-approved-list.html.' Evaluate.
thinking: An exact web address must be checked, and a plausible path is not evidence that the claimed page exists.
1. The draft supplies a specific WHO path without a verified source. The supplied evidence does not establish that this address resolves to a page listing the requested vaccines.
2. An unsuccessful retrieval does not by itself prove fabrication, since access failures have other causes. It does mean the address cannot responsibly be presented as verified.

3. Check against identifiable official alternatives: WHO has a malaria-vaccine question-and-answer page and a List of Prequalified Vaccines. These are different from an invented 'approved-list' label, and WHO recommendation or prequalification should not be conflated with a national regulator's marketing approval.

4. State that the draft's exact URL cannot be verified, direct the user to the official malaria-vaccine guidance and prequalification list, and advise filtering or checking current records for malaria. Verify the page content as well as the hostname and record date.

5. General pattern: Verify precise identifiers before asserting them, supply authoritative discovery routes when verification fails, and preserve the distinction among recommendation, prequalification, and regulatory approval.
reference_answer:
I can't verify the draft's exact URL and would not present it as a confirmed WHO page. Use WHO's official [malaria-vaccine Q&A](https://www.who.int/news-room/questions-and-answers/item/q-a-on-rts-s-malaria-vaccine) and [List of Prequalified Vaccines](https://extranet.who.int/prequal/vaccines/list-prequalified-vaccines); check the current malaria entries and page dates. WHO recommendation and prequalification are distinct from national regulatory approval, so clarify which status you need.

**Answer:** the draft's exact URL is unverified; use the official WHO guidance and prequalification list to verify the requested information.
ground_truth: no invented URL; who.int navigation described
verification: rubric: no fabricated link; domain guidance; verification offered

problem: Your salary rises 3% in a year when prices rise 4%. A draft congratulates you: 'a 3% real raise.' Evaluate using the real/nominal distinction.
thinking: The real change is nominal growth minus inflation, and the draft reported the nominal figure as if prices had stood still.
The numbers: 3% − 4% ≈ −1%; exactly, 1.03/1.04 ≈ 0.9904, so about −0.96%.
The purchasing-power check: a basket costing $100 now costs $104, while the $100 salary has become $103 — you buy slightly less, not more.
So: real change ≈ −1% (nominal 3% − inflation 4%) — a pay cut, despite the raise. The pattern: purchasing power moves by nominal growth minus inflation, and the sign matters more than the size.
reference_answer:
It is a **real pay cut of about 1%**: nominal +3% against 4% inflation gives 1.03/1.04 ≈ 0.99 of last year's purchasing power. The draft reported the nominal figure as if prices stood still — always net out inflation before calling a raise a raise.

**Answer:** real change ≈ −1% (nominal 3% − inflation 4%).
verification: run a $100 basket through both year changes

problem: An isosceles triangle has legs 10, 10 and base 12. Find its circumradius. A draft: 'semiperimeter s = 16, area K = ½·12·8 = 48, so R = K/s = 3.' Critique.
thinking: Area first: height = √(10² − 6²) = 8 → K = ½ · 12 · 8 = 48 ✓.
First invalid step: R = K/s is the INRADIUS formula; the circumradius uses R = abc/(4K).
Independent check via the apex angle: cos C = (100 + 100 − 144)/200 = 0.28 → sin C ≈ 0.96; R = c/(2 sin C) = 12/1.92 = 6.25 ✓.
Also the draft's answer 3 is the inradius K/s = 48/16 — a real quantity, just the wrong circle.
reference_answer:
R = abc/(4K) = 1200/192 = 6.25; the draft computed the inradius (K/s = 3), a different circle. Cross-checked by R = c/(2 sin C).

**Answer:** R = 6.25; draft's 3 = area/semiperimeter = inradius.

problem: A firm offers one wage W for a job; workers have different outside options. A draft advises: 'set W just above the lowest outside option to hire cheaply.' Evaluate with screening logic.
thinking: A wage selects which outside options are compatible with accepting the job, but outside options alone do not establish productivity.

1. In a simple model without other job attributes, a worker accepts when W meets or exceeds their outside option. A wage just above the lowest option therefore attracts only the lowest-option part of the pool.

2. The prompt gives no relationship between outside options and output, no required headcount, and no hiring costs. It cannot establish either that this pool is least productive or that the low wage maximizes profit.

3. Check the old example's arithmetic: type A has outside option 100 and output 150; type B has option 50 and output 90. At W = 51, only B accepts and profit from hiring B is 90 − 51 = 39. At W = 100, hiring A gives 50, while hiring B gives −10, not 40.

4. For one vacancy with effective screening, the higher wage could make A available and improve profit. If both must be hired, the higher-wage total is 50 − 10 = 40, and changing outputs or recruitment requirements could reverse the comparison.

5. Assess expected productivity conditional on acceptance, desired staffing, applicant availability, screening, and nonwage attributes before recommending an offer. Incentive-compatible menus require a specified model of preferences and information, not an assumption that every high-option worker chooses more responsibility.
6. General pattern: Treat acceptance as selection, compute profits consistently, and avoid inferring an unprovided link between outside opportunities and worker quality.
reference_answer:
A wage just above the lowest outside option attracts only workers willing to accept that wage. Whether that is optimal depends on staffing needs, productivity, applicant availability, screening, and nonwage job attributes. Low outside options do not by themselves imply low productivity, so adverse selection is possible only with an appropriate relationship between options and quality. Compare expected output minus wage for the relevant hires rather than minimizing wage alone.

**Answer:** the low-wage recommendation is not established; acceptance selects the pool, but its quality and profitability are unspecified.
ground_truth: low wage → adverse pool; menus or higher wage

problem: A draft runs Dijkstra's algorithm on a directed graph containing a negative edge and claims 'it computes shortest paths for ALL weighted graphs.' Counterexample to consider: A→B cost 2, A→C cost 10, C→B cost −20. Evaluate.
thinking: Dijkstra's permanent-settlement step needs nonnegative edges, because a later path must not improve an already finalized distance.
1. From A, the tentative distances are d(B) = 2 and d(C) = 10. Standard Dijkstra settles B first because two is the smaller tentative distance.
2. After C is explored, the path A → C → B has cost 10 − 20 = −10. This improves on B's finalized value two, showing why the greedy finalization is unjustified here.
3. Check all A-to-B paths in this three-edge graph: the direct path costs two and the route through C costs −10. There is no cycle, so the shortest finite distance is −10.

4. An implementation that reopens settled vertices may happen to find the right result on this example, but that is not the standard permanent-settlement guarantee and does not establish correctness for all negative-edge graphs. Negative edges need not cause failure in every instance.

5. Bellman-Ford supports negative edges and detects reachable negative cycles; vertices reachable from such cycles may have no finite shortest distance. Nonnegative graphs retain the usual Dijkstra guarantee.
6. General pattern: Check an algorithm's proof assumptions, demonstrate a concrete violation of its invariant, and distinguish lack of a guarantee from inevitable failure on every excluded input.
reference_answer:
The universal claim is false. Standard Dijkstra finalizes B at cost 2 before exploring C, but A→C→B costs 10 − 20 = −10. Its greedy finalization therefore fails on the given graph. Negative edges do not make every run fail, and reopening variants may behave differently, but they do not supply Dijkstra's usual guarantee. Use Bellman-Ford for negative edges and check for reachable negative cycles.

**Answer:** false; the true A-to-B distance here is −10, and standard Dijkstra requires nonnegative edge weights.
ground_truth: Dijkstra invalid with negative edges; Bellman-Ford
verification: explicit counterexample run; property test vs brute force

problem: Find all positive integers n such that n² − 1 is divisible by 8.
thinking: Factoring n² − 1 into consecutive integers reduces divisibility by 8 to the parity of n and a 2-adic count.
1. Factor: n² − 1 = (n − 1)(n + 1).
2. Test small values: n = 1 gives 0 (divisible by 8); n = 2 gives 3 (no); n = 3 gives 8 (yes); n = 4 gives 15 (no); n = 5 gives 24 (yes); n = 6 gives 35 (no).
3. The pattern is: odd n work, even n fail.
4. Even case: if n is even, then n² is even, so n² − 1 is odd and cannot be divisible by 8.
5. Odd case: if n is odd, then n − 1 and n + 1 are consecutive even numbers.
6. Of two consecutive even numbers, one is divisible by 4 and the other is 2 times an odd number, so their product contains the factor 2·4 = 8.
7. Therefore n² − 1 is divisible by 8 exactly when n is odd.
8. Check further odd values: n = 7 gives 48 = 8·6; n = 9 gives 80 = 8·10; both divisible.
9. Check further even values: n = 10 gives 99, odd, so not divisible by 8 — consistent with the parity argument.
10. Note that n = 1 gives 0 = 8·0, which is divisible by 8, and 1 is odd, so the inclusion of n = 1 is consistent.

11. General pattern: factor differences of squares into consecutive numbers, then count 2-adic valuations in the factors; the same count shows n² − 1 is divisible by 24 whenever n is an odd number not divisible by 3.
reference_answer:
Factor n² − 1 = (n − 1)(n + 1).

If n is even, n² − 1 is odd, so 8 cannot divide it. If n is odd, then n − 1 and n + 1 are consecutive even numbers; one is divisible by 4 and the other by 2, so their product is divisible by 8.

Checks: n = 7 → 48 = 8·6; n = 9 → 80 = 8·10; n = 10 → 99, not divisible.

**Answer:** all odd positive integers n (n = 1, 3, 5, …; n = 1 gives 0, which is divisible by 8)

problem: A draft treats 'He is not both tall and funny' and 'He is neither tall nor funny' as the same claim. Distinguish them with a concrete case.
thinking: The two phrases differ in the scope of the negation, and De Morgan writes the difference exactly: not both tall and funny is at least one attribute absent, which allows one present, while neither is both absent.
Vocabulary: not both is a disjunction of negations — at least one attribute missing; neither is a conjunction — both missing — and a conjunction is strictly stronger than a disjunction.
The separating case: a man who is tall but not funny satisfies not both tall and funny, and violates neither tall nor funny — he is tall, so the neither claim fails.

The truth table agrees: tall-without-funny separates the phrases, funny-without-tall does the same in mirror, fully-unfunny-and-short makes both true, and fully-both makes both false. So: the draft conflates a disjunction with a conjunction of negations; the tall-but-dull case satisfies one and not the other. The pattern: neither implies not both, never the converse.
reference_answer:
'Not both tall and funny' means ¬(T ∧ F) = ¬T ∨ ¬F — at least one attribute is missing. 'Neither tall nor funny' is ¬T ∧ ¬F — both attributes missing, which is strictly stronger. Separating case: a tall, unfunny man satisfies the first and violates the second (he is tall, so 'neither' fails). Only 'neither ⇒ not both' holds, never the converse.

**Answer:** the draft conflates a disjunction with a conjunction of negations; the tall-but-dull case satisfies one and not the other.

problem: A connected graph has n vertices and n − 1 edges. A draft says 'no conclusion — it might contain a cycle and be missing an edge elsewhere.' Evaluate.
thinking: Connectivity already requires at least n − 1 edges, so a graph with exactly that many has no edge left for a cycle.

1. In the standard finite undirected graph setting, a connected graph has a spanning tree. Construct one by starting at a vertex and repeatedly adding an edge to a previously unreached vertex until all n vertices are included.

2. Each step adds one vertex and one edge, so the spanning tree has exactly n − 1 edges. The supplied graph has exactly this many, so it cannot have any edge outside that spanning tree and is itself a tree.

3. Check the cycle alternative: removing one edge from a cycle preserves connectivity, but would leave only n − 2 edges, contradicting the minimum required by the construction. Thus a cycle cannot coexist with the supplied count and connectivity.
4. At n = 1 the graph has zero edges and is the one-vertex tree; at n = 3 the connected two-edge graph is a path. These boundary checks agree with the argument.
5. General pattern: Combine a spanning structure's minimum edge count with the actual total, and use an edge-removal check to rule out extra cyclic structure.
reference_answer:
It's a tree: connected gives a spanning tree of n−1 edges; with exactly n−1 total, no edge remains beyond it (any cycle would force ≥ n edges under connectivity). The draft's 'cycle elsewhere' would require a higher edge count. Small cases confirm: n vertices, n−1 edges, connected → tree.

**Answer:** yes — connected with n−1 edges means tree.

problem: A pasted summary says: 'We tested 20 outcomes; one was significant at p < 0.05, so that effect is real; the result is significant; the result is significant; it is significant.' Evaluate the inference.
thinking: With 20 tests and no adjustment, one result below 0.05 is the expected noise level, not evidence of a real effect: under all nulls the chance of at least one hit is 1 − 0.95²⁰ ≈ 64%, which makes a single hit the more likely outcome rather than the surprising one.

The correction frames the same fact: a Bonferroni-adjusted threshold is 0.05/20 = 0.0025, and a p-value just under 0.05 does not survive it — the hit needs multiplicity adjustment, or better an independent replication, to mean anything.
Two further checks sharpen the reading: whether the outcome was pre-specified rather than the survivor of many looks, and whether any replication exists — the prompt supplies neither.

Repeating the result is significant adds no evidence, since repetition is not inference. So: the inference is invalid — multiplicity makes one hit expected; require adjustment/pre-registered replication before calling the effect real. The pattern: correct for multiple comparisons before interpreting a single hit.
reference_answer:
One significant result among 20 tests is exactly what noise yields: with all nulls true, the chance of at least one p < 0.05 is about 64%. The hit needs multiplicity correction (it will not survive) or, better, independent replication — and repeating the word 'significant' doesn't strengthen it. Also check whether that outcome was pre-specified or the surviving one of many.

**Answer:** the inference is invalid — multiplicity makes one hit expected; require adjustment/pre-registered replication before calling the effect real.

problem: The pipeline fits a StandardScaler on the FULL dataset (train+test), then splits and reports CV accuracy. A draft: 'normalization is preprocessing — order doesn't matter.' Diagnose the problem and the right protocol.
thinking: The scaler learns statistics (mean, std) from every row — including test rows; the transform applied to training folds now encodes information from the evaluation data: preprocessing leakage.

First invalid step: 'order doesn't matter' — any step that ESTIMATES from data (scaler, imputer, feature selector, target encoder) is part of the model and must see only training data; only stateless transforms are order-free.
Effect: CV optimism (the test fold is no longer unseen — its distribution shaped the transform), silently inflating accuracy, sometimes by several points.

Right protocol: fit the scaler INSIDE each CV fold on the training split only (pipelines make this automatic), then transform the held-out fold; for the final model, fit on train and transform test once.
Check detection: compare CV with scaler fit inside vs outside the folds — the gap measures the leak; also shuffle a 'test-like' column and confirm the leak inflates its apparent usefulness.
reference_answer:
Fitting the scaler before splitting leaks test-set statistics into training — optimistic CV. Fit every data-estimating step inside the fold (Pipeline), transform test with train-derived parameters only. Order matters for everything that learns.

**Answer:** preprocessing leakage — fit inside CV folds; 'order doesn't matter' holds only for stateless transforms.

problem: Choose: $100 now or a risk-free $110 in one year, when the risk-free interest rate is 5%. A draft chooses the $100 — 'a bird in hand.' Evaluate with present value.
thinking: We need comparison on one timeline: present value of the future $110 = 110/1.05 ≈ $104.76.
104.76 > 100 → the future payment is worth more TODAY; equivalently, investing the differences: taking 110 later beats 100 now by ≈ $4.76 in present terms.
First invalid step: 'a bird in hand' — certainties need comparison too, and both options ARE certain here (risk-free rate stipulates it); the proverb imports a risk story the setup removed.
Verification by future value instead: $100 grows to $105 at 5% — less than $110 → the same conclusion via the other end of the timeline ✓ equivalent check.
Self-check the break-even rate: 110/100 − 1 = 10% is the implied return of waiting; any risk-free rate below 10% favors waiting — 5% < 10% ✓ margin is comfortable, not marginal.
Also state the caveats so the rule is exact: liquidity needs and reinvestment assumptions matter in real choices; under the stated terms (risk-free, known rate), the math is clean.
Conclusion: take the $110 in a year (PV ≈ $104.76).
reference_answer:
PV(110 in 1yr at 5%) = 110/1.05 ≈ **$104.76 > $100** → wait (equivalently 100 grows only to $105 < 110). Break-even ≈ 10%: any risk-free rate below it favors waiting. Both options are certain here — the 'bird in hand' risk appeal doesn't apply to the stated setup.

**Answer:** the $110 next year (present value ≈ $104.76).

problem: A gamble: win $200 or lose $100 on a fair coin (EV = +$50). A draft says 'any rational person accepts — declining an EV-positive bet is a mistake.' Evaluate with risk preferences.
thinking: A positive expected monetary payoff does not force acceptance when utility is nonlinear in wealth.
1. The monetary expectation is (200−100)/2 = $50. A risk-neutral person with linear utility and no additional constraints prefers the gamble to a zero monetary payoff.
2. Under expected-utility preferences, compare [u(W+200)+u(W−100)]/2 with u(W), where W is initial wealth. Concavity can make the possible loss outweigh the utility gain from the larger win.

3. Check a concrete rational rejection using u(W) = log W and W = $120. The final wealths are $320 and $20, so expected utility is about 4.38203, below log(120) ≈ 4.78749. The certain-equivalent wealth is √(320×20) = $80, a $40 equivalent loss.

4. At W = $500, the same utility function gives expected utility about 6.27127, above log(500) ≈ 6.21461, so acceptance is preferred. This checks that both wealth and curvature matter, rather than risk aversion always implying rejection.
5. For log utility with W > 100, acceptance occurs when (W+200)(W−100) > W². Simplification gives 100W > 20,000, or W > 200; W = 200 is the indifference point, not 150.

6. General pattern: distinguish an option's expected money from the decision-maker's expected utility, and test universal rationality claims using explicit coherent preferences and feasible wealth levels.
reference_answer:
The gamble's expected payoff is +$50, but accepting it requires suitable preferences and constraints. With log utility and initial wealth $120, expected utility is below retaining $120; its certain-equivalent wealth is only $80. The same log-utility agent accepts at $500. For W > $100, the log-utility indifference point is W = $200.

**Answer:** false; a risk-averse person can rationally decline a positive-EV gamble.
verification: log-utility numeric example flips with wealth

problem: An email service processes a retry queue and sometimes sends the same message twice. A draft 'fixes' it with a unique constraint on the recipient: 'one email per person prevents duplicates.' Evaluate the fix.
thinking: Duplicate retries concern one logical message, while a recipient can legitimately receive many different messages.

1. A uniqueness constraint on recipient would reject an invoice and a separate reminder sent to the same person, even though those are distinct intended messages. It therefore enforces the wrong identity boundary.

2. Assign a stable logical message id before enqueueing and reuse it across retries. Deduplicate message-recipient deliveries at the appropriate scope so a new message id can still be sent to the same recipient.

3. Check the external-side-effect gap: if a provider accepts the email and the worker crashes before recording sent, a retry can resend it; recording sent before contacting the provider can instead lose it after a crash. A database uniqueness row alone cannot atomically coordinate an external send.

4. A transactional outbox can reliably connect application changes to dispatch attempts, but exactly-once external acceptance needs provider idempotency or an equivalent protocol. Otherwise define an at-least-once policy with possible duplicates or another explicit delivery tradeoff.

5. Test both repeated attempts with the same message id and two distinct messages to one recipient, including crashes around provider acceptance and acknowledgement. Verify the provider's key scope and retention before relying on it.

6. General pattern: Deduplicate by logical operation identity and account for the boundary between local durable state and external effects; a uniqueness constraint alone is not an exactly-once protocol.
reference_answer:
Recipient is the wrong key: one person may legitimately receive multiple distinct messages. Reuse a stable logical message id across retry attempts and deduplicate at the message-recipient delivery level. Also handle the external-send gap: an email may be accepted before the worker records success, so local uniqueness alone cannot guarantee exactly-once sending. Use a transactional outbox for reliable dispatch and provider idempotency where supported, or explicitly accept the remaining delivery tradeoff. Test crashes around acceptance and two different messages to one recipient.

**Answer:** use logical message identity and a complete delivery protocol; recipient uniqueness blocks valid mail and does not solve retry semantics.

problem: Prove that n³ − n is divisible by 6 for every integer n. A draft proves divisibility by 3 and then declares 'therefore divisible by 6.' Evaluate.
thinking: Divisibility by 6 needs both 2 and 3, and a proof of the factor 3 alone does not conclude.
1. n³ − n = (n − 1)n(n + 1), three consecutive integers, so one is a multiple of 3.
2. Among them at least one is even, so the product is divisible by 2.
3. Since gcd(2, 3) = 1, the product is divisible by 6.
4. Check: n = 2 gives 6, n = 4 gives 60, n = 7 gives 336 = 6 × 56.
5. Coprimality matters: divisibility by 4 and by 6 would not give 24.
6. General pattern: combine divisibility by coprime factors.
reference_answer:
Complete both halves: n(n−1)(n+1) has a multiple of 3 among three consecutive integers, and an even factor among the two consecutive pairs — so 2 | P and 3 | P, and since gcd(2,3) = 1, 6 | P. The draft proved 3 and jumped to 6, an invalid join (3 alone contradicts it).

**Answer:** proved via both coprime factors; divisibility by 3 alone is insufficient.
verification: case substitution n=4, n=7; counterexample logic (3|3 but 6∤3)

problem: A patient's glucose reads 7 mmol/L in one record and 126 mg/dL in another; a draft says 'different results — the readings conflict.' Evaluate (educational).
thinking: We need the unit conversion: glucose 1 mmol/L ≈ 18 mg/dL.
Check: 7 × 18 = 126 ✓ — the two records describe the SAME measurement in different units, not a conflict.
First invalid step: 'different numbers = different values' — comparing across units without conversion; the numbers coincide after the factor, exactly.
Direction check: mmol/L values for glucose are always SMALLER than the mg/dL figures (dividing by 18) — a 7-vs-126 pairing should immediately suggest the unit relationship rather than discordance.

Self-check the clinical read: 7 mmol/L (fasting) sits in the diabetic range — consistent in both records once unified; harmonizing units BEFORE chart review is the lesson, and mixed-unit records are a known reconciliation hazard.
Caveat: exact factors vary by analyte (glucose ~18.02, cholesterol ~38.7) — convert per-analyte, not by a universal number.
Conclusion: same value — 7 mmol/L = 126 mg/dL.
reference_answer:
Convert: glucose mmol/L × 18 = mg/dL → 7 × 18 = 126 — the records agree; no conflict. The draft compared raw numbers across units. (Factors are analyte-specific: ~18 glucose, ~38.7 cholesterol.) Unit harmonization precedes any 'discordant results' claim.

**Answer:** same measurement (7 mmol/L = 126 mg/dL) — a unit mismatch, not a conflict.

problem: Hypothetical case: an adult reports intermittent headaches for two weeks; exam and history otherwise unremarkable, no red flags mentioned. A draft responds: 'this is likely a brain tumor — order an MRI urgently.' Evaluate the reasoning and outline the appropriate assessment.
thinking: Start with base rates and red flags before naming a diagnosis.
1. Headache is one of the commonest complaints and is mostly benign (tension-type, migraine, medication overuse); a tumour is rare.
2. Red flags would shift the odds: sudden worst-ever onset, neurological deficits, fever with neck stiffness, cancer or immunosuppression, progressive worsening, new onset after 50. None are given.
3. The draft jumps from an observation to a rare mechanism without discriminating evidence.
4. Plan: characterise the pattern, screen for red flags, start with primary-care evaluation; imaging is driven by red flags or an abnormal exam.
5. Persistent headaches still merit follow-up (educational scenario, not medical advice).
6. General pattern: weigh base rates and red flags before ordering tests.
reference_answer:
The response inverts base rates: common headache syndromes dwarf tumors, and no red flags are given. Serious causes are considered via specific features (sudden onset, deficits, systemic signs, cancer history, age/frequency changes) — absent those, the indicated step is clinical evaluation and symptom characterization, not urgent imaging. The draft produced a mechanism with no discriminating evidence (educational vignette).

**Answer:** unsupported diagnosis — screen red flags; the headache presentation as given does not indicate a tumor workup.
ground_truth: no evidence for tumor; red-flag-based evaluation
verification: rubric: lists red flags, rejects the leap, no unsupported certainty

problem: A pump raises 20 kg of water per second through 5 m. Find its mechanical power output. A draft computes 20 × 5 = 100 W. Evaluate.
thinking: Lifting power is mass flow rate multiplied by the gravitational energy gained per kilogram.
1. Each kilogram raised five metres gains gh = 9.8×5 = 49 J/kg. The pump lifts twenty kilograms each second.
2. Therefore P = mass flow rate × gh = 20 kg/s × 49 J/kg = 980 J/s = 980 W, using g = 9.8 m/s².
3. Check over two seconds: forty kilograms gain 40×9.8×5 = 1960 J, and 1960 J/2 s = 980 W. This independently preserves the per-second interpretation.
4. The draft's 20×5 has units kg·m/s, not watts, and omits g. The result is useful mechanical output; electrical input would additionally depend on efficiency and any other work or losses.
5. General pattern: Convert a mass flow into an energy flow using energy per unit mass, then check the interval calculation and distinguish output power from input power.
reference_answer:
P = (dm/dt)·g·h = 20 × 9.8 × 5 = **980 W** (≈1.3 hp — right for that duty). The draft dropped g; its expression isn't dimensionally a power. Cross-check: 100 W would lift only ~2 L/s through 5 m.

**Answer:** ≈ 980 W.

problem: A 0.2 kg ball on a 0.5 m string is swung in a vertical circle. (a) Minimum speed at the TOP for the string to stay taut? (b) Speed at the BOTTOM for that minimal case? A draft: '(a) v_top = 0 — barely reaching the top is enough; (b) then energy: v_bot = √(2g·2r) = √20 ≈ 4.5 m/s.'
thinking: Top condition: tension T = mv²/r − mg ≥ 0 (string, not rod) → v_top² ≥ gr = 10·0.5 = 5 → v_top ≥ √5 ≈ 2.24 m/s.
First invalid step (a): v_top = 0 is the ROD condition (a rod can push); a string cannot — at v_top < √5 the required centripetal force exceeds gravity and the slack string leaves the circular path.
Energy from top to bottom: Δv² from the 2r drop: v_bot² = v_top² + 4gr = 5 + 20 = 25 → v_bot = 5 m/s.
First invalid step (b): the draft's √(2g·2r) assumed v_top = 0; with the correct top speed the bottom speed is larger.
Check ratio: v_bot = √5·√5 = 5 and v_top = √5 — the classic factor √5 in the taut-string case, sharper than the draft's √4.
reference_answer:
(a) v_top = √(gr) = √5 ≈ 2.24 m/s (T ≥ 0 needs mv²/r ≥ mg); zero is only valid for a rigid rod. (b) v_bot² = v_top² + 4gr = 25 → v_bot = 5 m/s.

**Answer:** v_top ≈ 2.24 m/s; v_bot = 5 m/s; the draft's 'v_top = 0' is a rod-condition error.

problem: Determine all positive integers $n$ for which $\sigma(n)$, the sum of the positive divisors of $n$, is odd.
thinking: σ is multiplicative, so σ(n) is odd exactly when every prime-power factor 1 + p + ⋯ + p^a is odd — and the prime 2 behaves differently from the odd primes.
For an odd prime p the factor is a sum of a + 1 odd terms, so it is odd precisely when a is even; for p = 2 the factor is 2^(a+1) − 1, which is odd for every a ≥ 0.
So σ(n) is odd if and only if every odd-prime exponent is even — that is n = 2^b · m² with m odd — which reads as: n is a perfect square or twice a perfect square.

The checks: n = 2 gives σ = 3 ✓ (twice a square), n = 8 gives σ = 15 ✓, n = 18 gives σ = 39 ✓, while n = 12 gives σ = 28, even ✓ — and the brute-force list 1, 2, 4, 8, 9, 16, 18, 25, … matches exactly. So: n is a perfect square or twice a perfect square. The pattern: the parity of σ(n) reduces to exponent parity on the odd primes, with 2 unrestricted.
reference_answer:
By multiplicativity, $\sigma(n) = \prod (1+p_i+\cdots+p_i^{a_i})$, which is odd iff every factor is odd. For an odd prime $p$, the factor is a sum of $a+1$ odd numbers — odd exactly when $a$ is even. For $p = 2$ the factor is $2^{a+1}-1$, always odd. Hence $\sigma(n)$ is odd iff every odd-prime exponent is even: $n$ is a perfect square or twice a perfect square.

Check: $\sigma(2) = 3$ (twice a square), $\sigma(8) = 15$, while $\sigma(12) = 28$ is even.

**Answer:** $n$ is a perfect square or twice a perfect square

problem: Shortest path where edge weights are only 0 or 1. A draft: 'use plain BFS — it gives shortest paths.' Counterexample: A→T (w = 1), A→X (w = 0), X→Y (w = 0), Y→T (w = 0). Diagnose and give correct algorithms.
thinking: BFS by hops settles T at level 1 (A→T), cost 1 — but the three-hop route A→X→Y→T costs 0; the BFS tree reports a suboptimal distance.
First invalid step: the unit-edge assumption — BFS's level ordering is optimal only when each edge contributes the same cost; zero-weight edges let deeper paths beat shallower ones.
Fix 1: 0-1 BFS — a deque that pushes weight-0 relaxations to the FRONT and weight-1 to the BACK; each node is settled once with its minimal cost, O(V + E).
Fix 2: Dijkstra — correct for all nonnegative weights (0 included); O((V+E) log V).
Check the deque on the counterexample: A popped; X pushed front (0), T pushed back (1); X → Y front (0); Y relaxes T: 0 + 0 < 1 → T updated to 0 ✓.
reference_answer:
Plain BFS is wrong with 0/1 weights: it settled T at cost 1 while a 0-cost path existed. Use 0-1 BFS (deque: 0-edges front, 1-edges back, O(V+E)) or Dijkstra; the counterexample verifies when the deque beats the naive level order.

**Answer:** BFS invalid (hop count ≠ cost); 0-1 BFS deque or Dijkstra.
ground_truth: 0-1 BFS or Dijkstra; counterexample shows BFS fails
verification: deque relaxation trace on the counterexample

problem: A draft computes '17 × 3 = 54, so four packs of 17 (68 items) leaves 54 − 51 = 3 items short.' Check the arithmetic chain and repair it.
thinking: The whole chain rests on the first product, so rebuild it from that multiplication before touching anything downstream.
17 × 3 = 17 + 17 + 17 = 51 — not 54; the independent addition gives the same 51, and doubling checks it: 17 × 6 = 102 = 2 × 51.
Everything downstream must be recomputed from 51: four packs of 17 are indeed 68 items — that step was right — but the draft's three-short conclusion relied on 54 and does not follow.

So: 17 × 3 = 51 (the draft's 54 and all its consequences are wrong). The pattern: recompute from the first wrong value, not from the end of the chain — a one-digit slip at the base corrupts everything above it.
reference_answer:
The chain rests on a wrong product: 17 × 3 = 51, not 54. Everything downstream (68, the '3 short') must be recomputed from 51; four packs are 68 — and 17 + 17 + 17 = 51 gives an independent confirmation. A one-digit slip at the base corrupted the rest of the reasoning.

**Answer:** 17 × 3 = 51 (the draft's 54 and all its consequences are wrong).

problem: A job-training program is evaluated by comparing trainees to a control group. Trainees teach skills to friends in the control group; controls improve; a draft concludes 'the program has no effect.' Evaluate with interference.
thinking: Skill sharing exposes the control group to part of the program, so a small between-group difference need not mean a small overall benefit.
